AI.motivation: Current social deduction game agents are predominantly text-based, overlooking the multimodal nature fundamental to human social interaction, creating a gap in creating truly human-like AI agents capable of nuanced social dynamics.
AI.method: CaM-Wolf integrates multimodal perception and generation: 1) processes video inputs from other players, 2) employs a causal-aware Reasoner trained via reinforcement learning to establish logical chains between observable behaviors and hidden roles, and 3) presents itself through an animated avatar.
AI.result: Experiments and user studies show that CaM-Wolf achieves superior agent gameplay performance and enhances the quality of human-AI interaction compared to text-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: This work represents a significant advancement towards creating more human-like AI agents capable of participating in nuanced social dynamics, with multimodal perception being crucial for true social interaction capabilities.

title: Top-$k$ Pareto Bandits: Hypervolume Regret for Multi-Objective Slate Selection
summary: We consider a stochastic multi-objective bandit problem where, at each round, the agent selects a slate of $k$ arms and observes their $d$-dimensional reward vectors under semi-bandit feedback. We do not aim at identifying a single optimal arm; instead, we consider the problem of maintaining a small set of actions that jointly approximate the Pareto frontier. We formalize this objective through the dominated hypervolume induced by the selected subset of arms, and define an $α$-approximate hypervolume regret with respect to the best size-$k$ subset achievable in hindsight, where $α= 1 - 1/e$ reflects the approximation guarantee of greedy maximization for monotone submodular functions. To address this problem, we introduce \textit{THV-UCB}, an optimistic algorithm that selects arms greedily based on optimistic estimates of their marginal hypervolume contributions. We establish a gap-free regret bound $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{nkT})$ that holds on every instance, together with a gap-dependent bound $\tilde{O}(nk^{2.5}/Δ_{\min})$ that becomes polylogarithmic in $T$ once the arms are sufficiently well separated. Our results provide theoretical support for using small subsets to approximate Pareto fronts in various multi-objective applications.

AI.tldr: THV-UCB: A greedy optimistic algorithm for multi-objective bandits that selects small subsets of arms to approximate the Pareto frontier using dominated hypervolume as the quality metric, achieving sublinear regret bounds.
AI.motivation: In multi-objective decision problems, we often need to approximate the entire Pareto frontier rather than find a single optimal arm. Real-world applications require maintaining a small representative set of actions that jointly approximate the optimal trade-offs across multiple objectives, which is more practical than tracking the full Pareto set.
AI.method: Introduces THV-UCB (Threshold Hypervolume UCB), an optimistic algorithm that selects a slate of k arms greedily based on optimistic estimates of their marginal contributions to dominated hypervolume. The approach uses semi-bandit feedback and leverages the approximation guarantee of greedy maximization for monotone submodular functions (α = 1 - 1/e).
AI.result: Establishes two regret bounds: (1) a gap-free bound of Õ(d√nkT) that holds on every instance, and (2) a gap-dependent bound of Õ(nk²·⁵/Δ_min) that becomes polylogarithmic in T when arms are sufficiently well separated. These results provide theoretical guarantees for using small subsets to approximate Pareto fronts.
AI.conclusion: The THV-UCB algorithm provides a principled approach for multi-objective exploration-exploitation by maintaining small subsets that approximate Pareto frontiers, with strong theoretical guarantees supporting practical applications across various multi-objective settings.

title: CG-World: A Large-Scale World-State Dataset and Protocol for World Models
summary: World models must learn the joint dynamics of states, actions, events, and observations, yet existing video, robotics, and simulation datasets usually capture only part of this structure. We introduce CG-World, a large-scale world-state dataset and protocol derived from industrial computer graphics production pipelines. CG-World explicitly records intermediate states, including multimodal semantics, spatial structure, skeletal and controller states, motion curves, camera and lighting parameters, physics caches, contact events, and multi-pass renderings. CG-World v1 contains approximately 850,000 temporally aligned segments of 1-5 seconds. It separates latent states, observations, relations, events, and branch metadata, and organizes them into unified spatiotemporal samples. To support intervention learning and counterfactual reasoning, CG-World defines a branch lineage covering factual trajectories, observation interventions, action interventions, mechanism interventions, and strict counterfactual branches, with intervention targets, invariants, and alternative outcomes explicitly recorded. We evaluate the dataset on geometry-conditioned video generation, action prediction, and closed-loop vision-language-action policy transfer. Results show that CG-World provides reusable structured supervision for controlled generation, action modeling, and embodied policy transfer. We plan to expand CG-World through continued data collection and community collaboration toward a shared data infrastructure for world models, Physical AI, and embodied intelligence.

AI.tldr: CG-World is a large-scale world-state dataset from computer graphics production pipelines that captures comprehensive intermediate states, interventions, and counterfactuals for training world models.
AI.motivation: Existing datasets for world models are limited in capturing the joint dynamics of states, actions, events, and observations. Current video, robotics, and simulation datasets usually capture only part of this structure, making it difficult to train comprehensive world models.
AI.method: The authors create CG-World by extracting data from industrial computer graphics production pipelines, explicitly recording intermediate states including multimodal semantics, spatial structure, skeletal/controller states, motion curves, camera/lighting parameters, physics caches, contact events, and multi-pass renderings. The dataset includes approximately 850,000 temporally aligned segments of 1-5 seconds, organized into unified spatiotemporal samples with separation of latent states, observations, relations, events, and branch metadata.
AI.result: CG-World v1 contains 850,000 segments and supports intervention learning through branch lineages covering factual trajectories, observation interventions, action interventions, mechanism interventions, and strict counterfactual branches. The dataset enables evaluation on geometry-conditioned video generation, action prediction, and closed-loop vision-language-action policy transfer.
AI.conclusion: CG-World provides reusable structured supervision for controlled generation, action modeling, and embodied policy transfer, serving as a valuable data infrastructure for world models, Physical AI, and embodied intelligence. The authors plan to expand the dataset through continued data collection and community collaboration.

title: FloDR: An invertible dimensionality reduction method based on a normalising flow
summary: It is common for two-dimensional embeddings of high-dimensional data to be read far beyond what they can support. Distances in and between clusters, the meaning behind empty spaces, and the amount of structure hidden at each point are generally invisible in the output of methods such as t-SNE and UMAP. This is because the information that could support the meaning of these properties is discarded during the optimisation process. Here, we present FloDR, a dimensionality reduction method that embeds data through an invertible normalising flow. While FloDR only uses the first two output coordinates to create a two-dimensional embedding, it retains the remaining coordinates rather than discarding them. In addition to the embedding, an exact inverse and an exact density are properties of a trained mapping, which enable diagnostic visualisations that are computed from the exact inverse of the model that drew the layout rather than from an approximate one. Specifically, we draw two fields, the conditional spread, which measures how much of the original data remains undetermined at each embedding position in input units, and the hidden contrast, which measures how much information about a labelled contrast the two plotted coordinates discard. Both fields are rendered with a prespecified test against a held out portion of the input data and a bootstrap confidence. A field that fails the test is reported as refused.

AI.tldr: FloDR is a novel dimensionality reduction method that uses invertible normalizing flows to create 2D embeddings while retaining all dimensions, enabling diagnostic visualizations of what information is lost in the reduction.
AI.motivation: Current 2D embedding methods like t-SNE and UMAP discard crucial information during optimization, making it impossible to understand what aspects of the visualization are meaningful versus artifacts of the reduction process.
AI.method: FloDR uses invertible normalizing flows to embed data, keeping only the first two output coordinates for visualization while retaining all dimensions. This enables computation of exact inverse and density properties for diagnostic visualizations including conditional spread and hidden contrast fields with statistical testing.
AI.result: FloDR produces diagnostic visualizations that quantify uncertainty and information loss in embeddings through two main fields: conditional spread (how much original data remains undetermined at each point) and hidden contrast (how much labeled contrast information is discarded), with statistical validation.
AI.conclusion: FloDR addresses critical limitations of existing dimensionality reduction methods by providing transparent diagnostics about what information is preserved versus lost, enabling users to understand the reliability and limitations of their 2D visualizations.

title: MultivationBench: A Benchmark for Multimodal Sequential Motivation Reasoning
comment: 31 pages, including appendices; 6 figures and 22 tables. Code: https://github.com/HKUST-KnowComp/MultivationBench
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models have sparked significant interest due to their potential for social intelligence; however, their ability to perform sequential motivation reasoning remains insufficiently studied. Existing evaluations predominantly examine static text or isolated visual snapshots, which do not reflect the cumulative nature of real-world behavioral drivers. To address this gap, we introduce MultivationBench, a benchmark designed to rigorously evaluate multimodal motivation reasoning within story-driven visual narratives. The benchmark builds upon established psychological frameworks - Maslow's hierarchy and Reiss's basic desires - and requires models to integrate accumulated multimodal context to infer evolving motivations. Results indicate that MultivationBench presents a significant challenge: all tested models struggle to maintain consistent motivation reasoning across sequential contexts, revealing a critical disconnect between static recognition capabilities and the dynamic reasoning essential for human-like social understanding.

AI.tldr: MultivationBench is a new benchmark for evaluating multimodal LLMs' ability to perform sequential motivation reasoning using story-driven visual narratives, revealing that current models struggle with dynamic reasoning despite good static recognition.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs show potential for social intelligence but their sequential motivation reasoning capabilities are insufficiently studied. Existing evaluations focus on static text or isolated visual snapshots, which don't capture the cumulative nature of real-world behavioral drivers that unfold over time in visual narratives.
AI.method: The authors introduce MultivationBench, a benchmark built on psychological frameworks (Maslow's hierarchy and Reiss's basic desires) that evaluates models' ability to integrate accumulated multimodal context to infer evolving motivations across story-driven visual narratives.
AI.result: MultivationBench presents a significant challenge: all tested models struggle to maintain consistent motivation reasoning across sequential contexts. There's a critical disconnect between models' static recognition capabilities and the dynamic reasoning needed for human-like social understanding.
AI.conclusion: Current multimodal LLMs lack the ability for sequential motivation reasoning despite their static recognition strengths, highlighting the need for benchmarks like MultivationBench to push toward more human-like social understanding in AI systems.

title: Entity Resolution in Practice: Lessons from a Self-Serve Pipeline
summary: We built and evaluated a self-serve entity resolution (ER) system on six benchmarks spanning 864 to 5M records, and three lessons emerged that are absent from existing ER literature. (1) No single matching algorithm wins everywhere - a self-serve pipeline cannot predict its next dataset, so we recommend training several algorithm families per dataset and letting an automatic bake-off pick the winner. (2) Precision and recall need separate fixes, not a shared threshold - precision needs hard rule-based vetoes, recall needs more diverse candidate retrieval. (3) One false-positive link can silently merge unrelated entities - assuming "A matches B" and "B matches C" implies "A matches C" lets a single bad link chain hundreds of records together, so every cross-group merge must be actively re-verified. We hope these lessons save practitioners the months of dead-end experiments that led us to them.

AI.tldr: Self-serve entity resolution system evaluation reveals three practical lessons: no single matching algorithm works everywhere (need algorithm bake-offs), precision/recall require separate fixes (vetoes for precision, diverse retrieval for recall), and false-positive links can cause silent merging errors requiring active re-verification of cross-group merges.
AI.motivation: To address practical challenges in building self-serve entity resolution systems, where existing literature lacks guidance on dealing with unpredictable datasets and preventing cascading errors in production environments.
AI.method: Built and evaluated a self-serve ER system across six benchmarks spanning datasets from 864 to 5M records, conducting empirical analysis to derive practical lessons from real-world implementation challenges.
AI.result: Three key findings emerged: (1) No universal matching algorithm - requires training multiple algorithm families and using automatic bake-offs; (2) Precision and recall need separate fixes (rule-based vetoes for precision, diverse candidate retrieval for recall); (3) False-positive links can chain hundreds of records through transitive merging, requiring active re-verification of cross-group merges.
AI.conclusion: These practical lessons from real-world ER system implementation fill gaps in existing literature and can save practitioners months of dead-end experimentation by addressing algorithm selection, separate precision/recall optimization, and prevention of silent merging errors in production ER pipelines.

title: EvoPINN: Agentic Discovery of Executable Algorithms for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for solving partial differential equations (PDEs), yet their performance heavily relies on the manual, trial-and-error engineering of neural representations, loss formulations, and optimization dynamics. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising avenue for automated design, unconstrained code generation often yields mathematically invalid or numerically unstable solutions under strict scientific computing constraints. To bridge this gap, we propose \textbf{EvoPINN}, an agentic framework that reformulates PINN development from labor-intensive manual design into a rigorous, execution-grounded algorithm discovery problem. EvoPINN navigates a modular search space by decoupling neural representations from training programs, utilizing an LLM agent to iteratively propose memory-conditioned programmatic modifications. To ensure scientific validity, all candidates undergo strict structural verification and budget-matched PDE evaluation. Extensive experiments across diverse PDE regimes (oscillatory, elliptic, dissipative, and nonlinear transport) demonstrate that EvoPINN discovers PDE-specialized learning algorithms that significantly reduce relative $L_{2}$ error compared to baselines. Crucially, EvoPINN autonomously invented SLRC-PINN, a novel architecture whose performance gains persist under rigorous parameter-matched comparisons, establishing the viability of execution-grounded agents for discovering genuinely new scientific computing mechanisms.

AI.tldr: EvoPINN is an agentic framework that uses LLMs to automatically discover valid, high-performance PINN algorithms through evolutionary search with structural verification and PDE evaluation, outperforming manual designs.
AI.motivation: PINNs require labor-intensive manual engineering of neural representations, loss functions, and optimization dynamics. Current LLM approaches often produce invalid or unstable solutions under scientific computing constraints, creating a gap between automation and scientific rigor.
AI.method: EvoPINN reformulates PINN development as an execution-grounded algorithm discovery problem. It uses an LLM agent to iteratively propose memory-conditioned programmatic modifications in a modular search space, with all candidates undergoing strict structural verification and budget-matched PDE evaluation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse PDE regimes (oscillatory, elliptic, dissipative, nonlinear transport) show EvoPINN discovers PDE-specialized learning algorithms that significantly reduce relative L2 error compared to baselines. It autonomously invented SLRC-PINN, a novel architecture whose performance gains persist under rigorous parameter-matched comparisons.
AI.conclusion: EvoPINN establishes the viability of execution-grounded agents for discovering genuinely new scientific computing mechanisms, transforming PINN development from manual engineering to automated, rigorous algorithm discovery.

title: Evidence-Ledger Adjudication for Claim-Evidence Traceability
summary: AI agents can draft claims faster than authors can check whether the cited or retrieved evidence supports them. We study evidence-ledger adjudication: a claim-evidence traceability workflow that pairs each claim with an evidence packet, assigns a support relation, and routes unsupported, contradicted, or mixed-evidence claims back to the author. The empirical core is a 2,335-row blind benchmark built from independent external labels in AVeriTeC, CLIMATE-FEVER, and SciFact. Gold relations and source evidence labels are hidden during prediction and joined only for scoring. On this benchmark, the agent evidence-ledger condition achieves 0.676 relation accuracy and 0.601 macro-F1, compared with 0.383 accuracy and 0.303 macro-F1 for the best non-agent baseline. It also routes 1270/1435 claims whose gold labels indicate contradiction, missing evidence, or mixed evidence, while routing 295/900 supported claims. These results show that evidence-ledger adjudication can turn heterogeneous evidence packets into an auditable traceability layer for AI-assisted writing.

AI.tldr: Evidence-ledger adjudication workflow improves claim verification for AI-assisted writing by pairing claims with evidence packets and routing problematic claims back to authors.
AI.motivation: AI agents generate claims faster than authors can verify evidence support, creating a need for automated evidence verification and traceability systems.
AI.method: Proposed evidence-ledger adjudication: creates claim-evidence traceability workflow, assigns support relations, routes unsupported/contradicted claims back to authors. Built 2,335-row benchmark from AVeriTeC, CLIMATE-FEVER, SciFact datasets with gold labels hidden during prediction.
AI.result: Agent evidence-ledger achieved 0.676 relation accuracy and 0.601 macro-F1 vs 0.383 accuracy and 0.303 macro-F1 for best non-agent baseline. Successfully routed 1270/1435 claims with contradiction/missing/mixed evidence and 295/900 supported claims.
AI.conclusion: Evidence-ledger adjudication can transform heterogeneous evidence packets into an auditable traceability layer for AI-assisted writing, improving claim verification.

title: RAGuard: A Layered Defense Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems Against Data Poisoning
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS ResponsibleFM 2025, AAAI FrontierIR 2026
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems ground large language models (LLMs) in external corpora, but this reliance exposes them to corpus poisoning: maliciously injected passages that manipulate retrieved evidence. We introduce RAGuard, a layered defense against \emph{factual} corpus-poisoning attacks on RAG pipelines. The first layer adversarially fine-tunes a dense retriever on synthetic poisoned documents (fabricated facts, contradictions, and reasoning traps), teaching it to downrank malicious passages before generation. The second layer, the Zero-Knowledge Inference Patch ZKIP, is a label-free, black-box filter: for each retrieved document, it performs a leave-one-out decode and scores the document by the semantic shift and output-entropy change that its removal induces. ZKIP requires no poison labels, no ground-truth answers, and no access to model internals; it compares the model's own answers under counterfactual contexts. On poisoned Natural Questions at 5--30\% poison ratios, adversarial retriever training alone reduces but does not eliminate attack success, while ZKIP drives the measured attack success rate to 0.000 in every defended configuration, keeping Recall@5 within 0.03 of the clean-corpus baseline. Supervised analyses on both Natural Questions and BEIR (NFCorpus) confirm that the counterfactual signals ZKIP relies on carry learnable poison structure. The defense costs $k{+}1$ generator passes per query ($6\times$ for $k{=}5$); we analyze batching and early-stopping approximations that reduce this overhead. We also show that keyword-preserving poisons leave lexical retrievers such as BM25 essentially unaffected, an observation that delineates the boundary of the threat model. Code, datasets, and evaluation harnesses are released for reproducibility.

AI.tldr: RAGuard is a two-layer defense system that protects RAG systems from factual corpus-poisoning attacks through adversarial retriever training and a zero-knowledge inference patch filter, achieving near-perfect defense with minimal impact on retrieval performance.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are vulnerable to corpus poisoning attacks where malicious passages manipulate retrieved evidence, compromising the factual accuracy and reliability of LLM outputs. Current defenses are insufficient against sophisticated factual poisoning attacks.
AI.method: Two-layer approach: 1) Adversarial fine-tuning of dense retrievers using synthetic poisoned documents (fabricated facts, contradictions, reasoning traps) to teach ranking of malicious passages; 2) Zero-Knowledge Inference Patch (ZKIP) - a label-free, black-box filter that scores documents based on semantic shift and output-entropy changes when documents are removed during leave-one-out decoding.
AI.result: On Natural Questions at 5-30% poison ratios, adversarial retriever training alone reduces but doesn't eliminate attacks, while ZKIP drives attack success rate to 0.000 in all defended configurations while keeping Recall@5 within 0.03 of clean-corpus baseline. Supervised analyses confirm learnable poison structure in ZKIP's counterfactual signals.
AI.conclusion: RAGuard provides effective defense against factual corpus-poisoning attacks with minimal performance overhead (k+1 generator passes per query), demonstrates robust performance across poison ratios, and shows that keyword-preserving poisons don't affect lexical retrievers like BM25, defining threat boundaries.

title: Eco3S: Complex Socio-Economic System Simulation via Agent-Based Models
summary: The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) has renewed interest in agent-based modeling (ABM). However, current LLM-based ABM research faces several key challenges: modeling evolving agent-environment interactions, enabling flexible counterfactual reasoning, and automating simulation workflows for scientific research. In this paper, we propose Eco3S, a socio-economic system simulation framework for economic research and policy analysis that addresses these challenges through three key mechanisms: (1) Co-evolving Environment Design, a bidirectional feedback loop where agents and the environment co-evolve, producing realistic emergent behaviors; (2) Structural Causal Simulation, a structural causal model (SCM)-inspired counterfactual mechanism that allows flexible interventions for diverse causal inference tasks; (3) Simulation-Analysis-Refinement Paradigm, a self-corrective mechanism that iteratively refines experimental designs based on prior simulation results. Experiments on diverse economic scenarios confirm \textit{Eco3S}'s effectiveness in replicating multiple established economic studies (canal decay, origins of governance, and information propagation) and phenomena across domains. Additional results further demonstrate its scalability and generalizability, highlighting the framework's potential for rigorous economic research and policy-making.

AI.tldr: Eco3S is a socio-economic simulation framework using LLM-based agents with co-evolving environments, causal counterfactual reasoning, and automated iterative refinement for economic research and policy analysis.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based agent-based modeling faces challenges in modeling evolving agent-environment interactions, enabling flexible counterfactual reasoning, and automating simulation workflows for scientific research.
AI.method: Eco3S introduces three key mechanisms: 1) Co-evolving Environment Design with bidirectional feedback between agents and environment, 2) Structural Causal Simulation inspired by SCMs for counterfactual reasoning, and 3) Simulation-Analysis-Refinement Paradigm for iterative self-correction of experiments.
AI.result: Experiments confirm Eco3S's effectiveness in replicating multiple established economic studies (canal decay, origins of governance, information propagation) and phenomena across domains, demonstrating scalability and generalizability.
AI.conclusion: Eco3S shows strong potential for rigorous economic research and policy-making by addressing key limitations in current LLM-based ABM approaches through its integrated framework of co-evolution, causal reasoning, and automated refinement.

title: Automorphism-Induced Non-Canonicity in Top-k Explanations of Graph Neural Networks
summary: A gradient-based GNN explainer given a molecule with two chemically equivalent nitro groups assigns them attribution scores that are equal to the last bit. It cannot do otherwise: message passing is exactly permutation equivariant, so any automorphism of the input leaves every attribution invariant. Yet the standard report, the top-k edges, names one of the two, and which one is settled by the order of an array. We show this is a structural obstruction rather than an implementation slip. When no minimal valid explanation is fixed by the input's automorphism group, no rule can be single-valued, minimal and symmetry-respecting at once. For the exact-k reports used in practice we give a parameter-free criterion, mechanised in Lean 4 with no axiom dependencies, that decides from the graph alone whether every score-optimal report of that size must split an orbit. Across 21298 instance-budget decisions the criterion agrees with a mechanical model-equivalence check without exception, and no severing case we found admitted a neutral alternative. The obstruction is common. Nontrivial automorphisms occur in 93.4% of Mutagenicity, the dataset the seminal explainability papers use, so the measure-zero dismissal of symmetric inputs, sound on the continuous domains it was made for, collapses here. At the sparsity budget those papers report, 24.0% of molecules with two interchangeable nitro groups (6 of 25) surface exactly one of them, every one arbitrary under mechanical verification. A model's blindness also manufactures symmetry: every MUTAG molecule contains atoms chemistry separates and the network provably cannot, and a matched control shows the resolution is set by what the model reads rather than how it is parameterised. Reporting orbits removes the arbitrariness at 0.11 ms and 0.43 extra edges per graph.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that GNN explainers for molecular graphs cannot simultaneously be single-valued, minimal, and symmetry-respecting due to structural obstructions from graph automorphisms, leading to arbitrary explanations for chemically equivalent structures.
AI.motivation: Gradient-based GNN explainers assign equal attribution scores to chemically equivalent groups (like two nitro groups) due to permutation equivariance, but standard reporting methods arbitrarily pick one for top-k explanations. This creates arbitrary explanations that don't respect chemical symmetry.
AI.method: The paper provides a parameter-free criterion (mechanized in Lean 4) that decides from the graph structure alone whether every score-optimal exact-k explanation must split an automorphism orbit. The method analyzes structural obstructions rather than implementation issues.
AI.result: The criterion shows that 24.0% of molecules with two interchangeable nitro groups surface exactly one arbitrary nitro group in explanations. Nontrivial automorphisms occur in 93.4% of Mutagenicity dataset molecules, and reporting whole orbits instead of individual elements removes arbitrariness with minimal computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: There's a fundamental trade-off between single-valued, minimal, and symmetry-respecting explanations in GNN attribution due to graph automorphisms. The problem is not implementation-specific but structural, requiring alternative reporting approaches like reporting entire orbits instead of individual elements.

title: Fewer Clarifications, Better Code: Benchmarking Cross-Session Personalized Ambiguity Adaptation in Coding Assistants
summary: AI-assisted coding increasingly translates informal user intent into executable software, yet coding requests often contain ambiguities that recur in user-specific ways across tasks and sessions. Existing disambiguation methods typically address each ambiguous request in isolation within the current coding session, often through eliciting additional clarification. However, whether resolved session history from the same user can serve as memory for resolving recurring personalized ambiguity in a newly opened session remains underexplored. We formulate personalized ambiguity adaptation as a new task: given a user's previously resolved coding sessions and a new ambiguous request, an assistant should identify the recurring ambiguity pattern, produce the intended executable solution, and minimize clarification. To benchmark this task, we introduce CAPA, which characterizes personalized coding ambiguity through six mechanisms and injects these mechanisms into unambiguous executable tasks using a controlled three-stage generation pipeline. CAPA contains 600 coding sessions across 60 balanced user--ambiguity cells, including 300 held-out evaluation sessions. We evaluate 12 recent LLMs under no-history and same-user-history conditions using executable success, first-turn success, and turns-to-completion. Our analyses examine task difficulty, user identity, and memory-based history use, and we further propose same-user history gating as a lightweight inference-time method. CAPA provides a foundation for developing long-term coding assistants that better align generated code with user intent while reducing repeated clarification.

AI.tldr: CAPA introduces a benchmark for personalized ambiguity adaptation in AI coding assistants, where models learn from users' resolved session histories to disambiguate recurring patterns in new sessions, reducing the need for repeated clarifications.
AI.motivation: Current AI coding assistants handle ambiguous requests in isolation within each session, requiring repeated clarification even when similar ambiguities recur for the same user across different sessions. There's an unexplored opportunity to leverage resolved session history from the same user as memory to resolve recurring personalized ambiguity patterns.
AI.method: The paper formulates personalized ambiguity adaptation as a new task, introduces the CAPA benchmark with 600 coding sessions across 60 user-ambiguity cells generated via controlled three-stage pipeline, and evaluates 12 recent LLMs under different history conditions with metrics like executable success, first-turn success, and turns-to-completion.
AI.result: The CAPA benchmark shows that using same-user history significantly improves performance over no-history conditions. The paper also proposes same-user history gating as a lightweight inference-time method for better memory-based history use, and analyzes task difficulty, user identity effects, and model performance variations.
AI.conclusion: CAPA establishes a foundation for developing long-term coding assistants that can better align generated code with user intent by learning from resolved session histories, reducing repeated clarification overhead while maintaining high-quality executable solutions.

title: MetaKoopman: Bayesian Meta-Learning of Koopman Operators for Modeling Structured Dynamics under Distribution Shifts
summary: Modeling and forecasting nonlinear dynamics under distribution shifts is essential for robust decision-making in real-world systems. In this work, we propose MetaKoopman, a Bayesian meta-learning framework for modeling nonlinear dynamics through linear latent representations. MetaKoopman learns a Matrix Normal-Inverse Wishart (MNIW) prior over the Koopman operator, enabling closed-form Bayesian updates conditioned on recent trajectory segments. Moreover, it provides a closed-form posterior predictive distribution over future state trajectories, capturing both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty in the learned dynamics. We evaluate MetaKoopman on a full-scale autonomous truck and trailer system across a wide range of adverse winter scenarios, including snow, ice, and mixed-friction conditions, as well as in simulated control tasks with diverse distribution shifts. MetaKoopman consistently outperforms prior approaches in multi-step prediction accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and robustness to distributional shifts. Field experiments further demonstrate its effectiveness in dynamically feasible motion planning, particularly during evasive maneuvers and operation at the limits of traction. Project website: https://mahmoud-selim.github.io/MetaKoopman/

AI.tldr: MetaKoopman: A Bayesian meta-learning framework that models nonlinear dynamics with linear Koopman operators, enabling closed-form Bayesian updates and uncertainty quantification for robust prediction under distribution shifts.
AI.motivation: Modeling and forecasting nonlinear dynamics under distribution shifts is crucial for robust decision-making in real-world systems, particularly in safety-critical applications like autonomous vehicles operating in varying conditions.
AI.method: Proposes MetaKoopman framework that learns a Matrix Normal-Inverse Wishart (MNIW) prior over Koopman operators, enabling closed-form Bayesian updates from trajectory segments and providing posterior predictive distributions capturing both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty.
AI.result: Outperforms prior approaches in multi-step prediction accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and robustness to distribution shifts on both real-world autonomous truck testing (snow, ice, mixed-friction conditions) and simulated control tasks with diverse distribution shifts.
AI.conclusion: MetaKoopman provides an effective Bayesian meta-learning approach for nonlinear dynamics modeling with uncertainty quantification, demonstrating practical value in safety-critical applications like autonomous vehicle motion planning, especially during challenging maneuvers and traction-limited operations.

title: AlphaSchema: Exploring the Space of Trading Semantics for LLM-Based Alpha Mining
summary: Automated alpha mining has increasingly adopted large language model (LLM) agents for factor generation and iterative discovery. However, existing LLM-based systems often delegate both factor construction and search decisions to the agent itself, without an explicit exploration space or a principled mechanism for navigating that space. As a result, exploration remains largely implicit and difficult to control or optimize systematically. We introduce AlphaSchema, which constructs and explores a structured space of trading semantics for alpha mining. Each point in this space is a schema plan composed of Event, Context, Qualities, Direction, and Output, specifying the semantics of a candidate factor before implementation. AlphaSchema decouples exploration from implementation: an LLM translates selected schema plans into executable factors, while evaluated rewards are accumulated to learn a surrogate model over the semantic space. An iterative selection mechanism uses this model to balance global exploration, surrogate-guided exploitation, and local mutation. Experiments on the Chinese stock market show that AlphaSchema discovers factor pools with strong predictive and portfolio performance. Further analyses show that the semantic search process navigates diverse regions while increasingly allocating evaluations toward high-reward regions, and that implementations of the same schema plans by different LLMs exhibit comparable predictive quality, suggesting that alpha mining quality is largely robust to the choice of LLM within our framework.

AI.tldr: AlphaSchema introduces a structured approach to alpha mining using LLMs, decoupling semantic exploration from factor implementation via schema plans and surrogate modeling for systematic search optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based alpha mining systems lack explicit exploration spaces and principled mechanisms for navigating them, making exploration implicit and difficult to control or optimize systematically.
AI.method: AlphaSchema constructs a structured semantic space with schema plans (Event, Context, Qualities, Direction, Output), decouples exploration from implementation using LLMs for translation, and uses iterative selection with surrogate modeling to balance exploration, exploitation, and local mutation.
AI.result: Experiments on the Chinese stock market show AlphaSchema discovers factor pools with strong predictive and portfolio performance. The semantic search process navigates diverse regions while allocating evaluations toward high-reward regions, and different LLMs implementing the same schema plans yield comparable predictive quality.
AI.conclusion: AlphaSchema provides a systematic framework for LLM-based alpha mining that improves exploration control and optimization, showing robustness to LLM choice while delivering strong performance in financial markets.

title: High-Order Markov Blanket Discovery via a k-Order Relaxation of the Faithfulness Assumption
comment: 17 pages (9 pages main text + supplementary material), 4 figures, 8 tables, 3 algorithms. Accepted at the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI 2026). Code: https://github.com/lklee9/k-order-Markov-blanket
summary: The problem of learning the graphical Markov blanket (MB) of a variable from data has applications in many areas such as structure learning for Bayesian networks and Markov random fields, causal discovery, and feature selection. However, a common assumption most methods make is that the conditional independencies in the distribution imply the same separation in the graphical structure -- also known as the faithfulness assumption. Unfortunately, this assumption can be violated by higher-order dependencies such as XOR and parity-type relations, and -- on finite samples -- by empirical violations that, in extreme cases, even induce spurious dependencies absent from the true distribution. Therefore, in this paper we propose a "k-order" relaxation of the faithfulness assumption that captures parity type relationships between k+2 variables. We then propose a proof of concept algorithm called k-order Markov blanket (kOMB) that uses this relaxation for MB discovery. Finally, we empirically show how kOMB can recover the MB of a variable under both true and empirical violations of faithfulness. Code available at: https://github.com/lklee9/k-order-Markov-blanket

AI.tldr: A novel k-order relaxation of the faithfulness assumption enables MB discovery even with XOR/parity-type dependencies, with proof-of-concept kOMB algorithm showing empirical recovery of MBs under faithfulness violations.
AI.motivation: The faithfulness assumption - that conditional independencies in distribution imply separation in graphical structure - is commonly violated by higher-order dependencies (like XOR/parity relations) and empirical violations in finite samples, making existing MB discovery methods unreliable.
AI.method: Proposes a "k-order" relaxation of faithfulness assumption capturing parity-type relationships between k+2 variables, then develops k-order Markov blanket (kOMB) algorithm that uses this relaxation for MB discovery.
AI.result: Empirical demonstration that kOMB can recover the Markov blanket of a variable under both true faithfulness violations (inherent in distribution) and empirical violations (due to finite samples).
AI.conclusion: The k-order faithfulness relaxation and kOMB algorithm provide a principled approach to MB discovery that works robustly even when traditional faithfulness assumptions are violated by complex dependencies.

title: Rethinking Self-Evolution: A Constrained Exploration-Exploitation Process for Mitigating Skill Overfitting
summary: Enabling large language model (LLM) agents to accumulate and reuse experience from past interactions remains a central challenge in real-world applications. A promising solution is to treat skills as trainable states and optimize them in the same way as model parameters in neural network training. However, data-driven skill optimization is prone to overfitting to the limited trajectories collected from real environments. Overexploiting these trajectories overfits the current batch, while unconstrained exploration causes regression on previously solved cases. This tension motivates a constrained search view of skill self-evolution, governed by an exploration--exploitation trade-off. We propose SkillBoost, a three-stage framework that mitigates both risks: structured exploitation localizes observed failures to editable skill components, prior-guided exploration draws on prior knowledge in the LLM to generate diverse repair candidates, and verified acceptance commits a candidate only when it improves performance within a regression bound. Experiments across 23 model--benchmark configurations show that SkillBoost achieves state-of-the-art performance while mitigating overfitting, outperforming both human-crafted and LLM-generated skills. Transfer experiments further show that optimized skills can be reused by other agents on similar tasks.

AI.tldr: SkillBoost is a three-stage framework that enables LLM agents to accumulate and reuse experience through skill self-evolution, addressing overfitting by balancing exploration-exploitation trade-offs during skill optimization.
AI.motivation: LLM agents struggle to accumulate and reuse experience from past interactions in real-world applications. Current skill optimization approaches suffer from overfitting to limited trajectories - overexploiting existing data leads to overfitting, while unconstrained exploration causes regression on previously solved problems.
AI.method: SkillBoost uses a three-stage framework: 1) Structured exploitation that localizes failures to editable skill components, 2) Prior-guided exploration that uses LLM's knowledge to generate diverse repair candidates, and 3) Verified acceptance that commits a candidate only when it improves performance within a regression bound.
AI.result: Experiments across 23 model-benchmark configurations show SkillBoost achieves state-of-the-art performance while mitigating overfitting, outperforming both human-crafted and LLM-generated skills. Transfer experiments demonstrate that optimized skills can be reused by other agents on similar tasks.
AI.conclusion: SkillBoost successfully addresses the skill optimization challenge in LLM agents through a constrained search approach that balances exploration and exploitation, enabling effective experience accumulation and reuse while preventing overfitting and regression.

title: Post-Training at the Edge of Detectability: A Game-Theoretic Approach to Fine-Tuning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning is widely used in language model training to improve model performance on a target task while limiting drift from a reference policy. A standard way to balance this trade-off is via a KL-regularized RL objective, although this formulation does not by itself provide a principled way to set the regularization coefficient. In practice, the coefficient is typically chosen heuristically or via hyperparameter search, which can lead to unnecessary overhead in training cost or undesirable reward-retention trade-offs. We instead propose a game-theoretic framework that gives this trade-off an explicit statistical interpretation. Specifically, we study a sequential game in which an agent chooses a policy to maximize cumulative reward while a monitor observes policy outputs over time and tests for deviations from the reference policy. Although not originating from the same perspective, we show that the resulting equilibrium policy can nonetheless be expressed as the solution to a KL-regularized RL problem for an optimal regularization parameter that can be viewed as maximizing reward per unit of statistical distinguishability. Drawing on classical results from concave-convex fractional programming, we provide a principled method for learning this equilibrium coefficient via reduction to the KL-regularized RL objective, thus allowing for flexible integration into standard fine-tuning pipelines. In experiments with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.2-1B, we demonstrate that our methods result in competitive reward-retention trade-offs in a continual learning setting, and illustrate how our framework may be used to audit API providers serving open-source models.

AI.tldr: A game-theoretic framework for principled KL-regularized RL fine-tuning that learns optimal regularization coefficients via sequential monitoring games, eliminating heuristic hyperparameter tuning.
AI.motivation: Current RL fine-tuning uses heuristic or hyperparameter search to set KL regularization coefficients, which is inefficient and can lead to suboptimal reward-retention trade-offs.
AI.method: Proposes a sequential game framework where an agent maximizes reward while a monitor tests for deviations from reference policy; shows equilibrium equals KL-regularized RL with optimal coefficient, solved via concave-convex fractional programming.
AI.result: Demonstrates competitive reward-retention trade-offs on Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.2-1B in continual learning, and shows framework can audit API providers serving open-source models.
AI.conclusion: Provides a principled, game-theoretic approach to KL-regularized RL fine-tuning that replaces heuristic coefficient selection with an optimal solution based on statistical distinguishability, enabling better performance and model auditing capabilities.

title: AgenticCANN: Automated Ascend C Operator Generation via Knowledge-Augmented Agentic Evolution
summary: Ascend C operator optimization is critical for NPU (Neural Processing Unit) inference performance but requires deep hardware expertise.While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automated CUDA kernel generation, the fundamentally different programming model of Ascend C introduces unique challenges that remain unexplored. In this paper, we propose AgenticCANN, a knowledge-augmented agentic evolution framework specifically tailored for automated Ascend C operator synthesis in low-corpus NPU environments.To overcome the severe platform knowledge deficit on unfamiliar hardware, AgenticCANN incorporates a knowledge-orchestrated generation system that delivers structured, multi-level domain insights across the development lifecycle to resolve the upstream feasibility bottleneck.Building on this foundation, it features a stage-adaptive agentic evolution strategy that dynamically aligns LLM interaction modes with specific generation and evolution phases, balancing high-exploration candidate discovery with high-convergence performance tuning.Extensive experiments on Huawei Ascend 910B across six operators spanning five pattern categories demonstrate that our method achieves 90 to 100 percent feasibility on elementwise and normalization operators, 56% on fusion operators, and up to 6.65$\times$ speedup on 1B Pangu model inference kernels. Further analysis reveals that knowledge injection monotonically improves feasibility from 57% to 86% on elementwise operators, demonstrating its general rather than operator-specific benefit.

AI.tldr: AgenticCANN is a knowledge-augmented AI agent framework that automatically generates optimized Ascend C operators for NPU inference, overcoming hardware expertise gaps through structured knowledge injection and adaptive evolution strategies.
AI.motivation: Ascend C operator optimization is critical for NPU inference performance but requires deep hardware expertise that's scarce. While LLMs show promise for CUDA kernel generation, Ascend C's fundamentally different programming model presents unexplored challenges, especially in low-corpus NPU environments.
AI.method: AgenticCANN features: 1) Knowledge-orchestrated generation system delivering structured, multi-level domain insights across development lifecycle to overcome hardware knowledge deficit; 2) Stage-adaptive agentic evolution strategy that dynamically aligns LLM interaction modes with specific generation phases, balancing exploration for candidate discovery with convergence for performance tuning.
AI.result: Experiments on Huawei Ascend 910B across 6 operators spanning 5 pattern categories show: 90-100% feasibility on elementwise/normalization operators, 56% on fusion operators, and up to 6.65× speedup on 1B Pangu model inference kernels. Knowledge injection monotonically improves feasibility from 57% to 86% on elementwise operators.
AI.conclusion: AgenticCANN successfully addresses the Ascend C operator synthesis challenge in low-corpus environments through knowledge-augmented agentic evolution, demonstrating that structured knowledge injection provides general rather than operator-specific benefits for overcoming hardware expertise deficits.

title: ClockRoPE: Random Fourier Rotations for Temporal Routine Modeling
summary: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) has been widely adopted in transformer-based large language models. However, its log-linear frequency schedule, originally designed to produce long-term attention decay, limits its adoption in domains with more complex distance-correlation patterns, such as temporal periodicity in sequential recommendation. We investigate the expressiveness of general query/key rotations and find that any normalized continuous positive-definite attention modulation function can be approximated by random rotations induced by its own Fourier transform, which we term Random Fourier Rotations. Building on this theory, we propose ClockRoPE for routine modeling in sequential recommendation, where rotation frequencies are derived from periodic attention modulation functions. In online A/B tests, ClockRoPE demonstrates consistent improvements in valued engagement metrics, and has been successfully deployed in production-scale generative retrieval system at a major video-sharing platform.

AI.tldr: ClockRoPE replaces RoPE's log-linear frequency schedule with periodic rotation frequencies from attention modulation functions, improving performance in sequential recommendation with routine patterns.
AI.motivation: RoPE's log-linear frequency schedule, designed for long-term attention decay, is insufficient for domains like sequential recommendation that exhibit complex distance-correlation patterns and temporal periodicity.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis shows any normalized continuous positive-definite attention modulation function can be approximated by random rotations from its Fourier transform (Random Fourier Rotations). Based on this, ClockRoPE derives rotation frequencies from periodic attention modulation functions for routine modeling.
AI.result: Online A/B tests show consistent improvements in valued engagement metrics. ClockRoPE has been successfully deployed in a production-scale generative retrieval system at a major video-sharing platform.
AI.conclusion: ClockRoPE extends RoPE's capabilities by enabling modeling of complex periodic patterns, making it suitable for sequential recommendation tasks with routine behaviors, and has proven effective in real-world deployment.

title: UrbanDS: A Graph-Guided LLM Multi-Agent System for Data-Intensive Urban Tasks
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have been widely applied in automating data science tasks. However, existing methods typically rely on a limited set of provided datasets, and they face challenges in data-intensive scenarios that require discovering and leveraging relevant information from large-scale and heterogeneous data repositories. Urban tasks are representative examples of such scenarios, as urban data are not only large-scale and multi-sourced, but also exhibit complex spatial, temporal, and semantic relationships. To address these challenges, we propose UrbanDS, a graph-guided LLM multi-agent system for data-intensive urban tasks. We first construct a unified dataset graph to organize reusable dataset skills and the relationships among datasets. Specifically, we develop a Data Profiling Agent that constructs a skill for each dataset. Moreover, a Relation Agent identifies relationships among datasets and integrates these relationships into the dataset graph. At runtime, a Planner Agent retrieves task-relevant datasets from the graph and generates execution plans. Multiple Execution Agents then perform data processing and analysis, while their execution progress and intermediate results are shared through a common memory. Finally, a Report Agent synthesizes the experimental logs into a report, which can be further refined based on user feedback. To systematically evaluate the capability of agents in handling data-intensive urban scenarios, we further construct UrbanDS-Bench, an urban data science benchmark covering representative data analysis and modeling tasks. Experiments on both general and urban benchmarks demonstrate that UrbanDS consistently outperforms existing data science agents on data-intensive tasks. Furthermore, UrbanDS has been deployed on the urban operations platform of Dongxihu District, Wuhan, demonstrating its effectiveness in real-world urban applications.

AI.tldr: UrbanDS is a graph-guided LLM multi-agent system that uses dataset graphs and specialized agents to handle data-intensive urban tasks by discovering and leveraging relationships among heterogeneous urban data.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agents for data science tasks are limited to provided datasets and struggle with data-intensive scenarios requiring discovery and utilization of information from large-scale, heterogeneous data repositories. Urban tasks are particularly challenging due to their large-scale, multi-sourced nature with complex spatial, temporal, and semantic relationships.
AI.method: UrbanDS constructs a unified dataset graph to organize reusable dataset skills and relationships. It uses specialized agents: Data Profiling Agent to create dataset skills, Relation Agent to identify dataset relationships, Planner Agent to retrieve task-relevant datasets and generate execution plans, multiple Execution Agents for data processing/analysis with shared memory, and Report Agent to synthesize experimental logs into reports.
AI.result: UrbanDS consistently outperforms existing data science agents on data-intensive tasks across both general and urban benchmarks. The system was also successfully deployed on the urban operations platform of Dongxihu District, Wuhan, demonstrating real-world effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: UrbanDS provides an effective solution for data-intensive urban scenarios by organizing datasets into graphs and employing specialized LLM agents for different aspects of the data science workflow, enabling better discovery and utilization of complex urban data relationships in both benchmark evaluations and real-world applications.

title: Q-Steer: Action-Value Guidance for Molecular Policy Optimization
comment: 20 pages, 2 figures, and 25 tables. Includes supplementary experimental results
summary: Oracle-limited molecular optimization gives reward only after a complete molecule is generated, while each rollout requires many local next-token decisions. This delayed-feedback interface makes molecular policy optimization myopic: an optimizer can learn that a molecule was good without knowing which intermediate actions made it good. We introduce Q-Steer, a rollout-time action-value steering primitive for molecular language models. Q-Steer uses an offline-trained and frozen prefix-action value scorer, PAVS-Q, that estimates the downstream reward of taking a candidate next token under a partial SMILES prefix, then adds a normalized value bonus to sampling logits. The optimizer update rule and online oracle budget are unchanged; the claim is fixed-online-oracle performance, not equal total compute. On PMO23 with a fixed 10,000-call online budget, complete factorial studies across two molecular language-model backbones and four optimizers show that Q-Steer improves mean valid-unique score in all eight backbone-optimizer cells, with positive macro mean-score gains between +0.033 and +0.049 and 18-20 task wins per cell. Mechanism controls show that action identity matters: prefix-broadcast values are nearly neutral, while shuffled action values harm performance. These results support Q-Steer as a reusable rollout-time action-value wrapper that improves average molecular optimization reward across optimizer families and policy backbones without changing the online oracle budget.

AI.tldr: Q-Steer improves molecular optimization by adding action-value guidance during rollouts, boosting performance without increasing online oracle budget
AI.motivation: Molecular optimization suffers from delayed feedback where only complete molecules get rewards, making policy optimization myopic - the optimizer learns which molecules are good but not which intermediate actions led to success
AI.method: Q-Steer uses an offline-trained prefix-action value scorer (PAVS-Q) that estimates downstream reward for candidate next tokens given partial SMILES prefixes, then adds normalized value bonuses to sampling logits during rollout
AI.result: On PMO23 with fixed 10,000-call online budget, Q-Steer improved mean valid-unique score across all 8 backbone-optimizer combinations (gains +0.033 to +0.049), with 18-20 task wins per cell; mechanism controls confirmed action-specific values are crucial
AI.conclusion: Q-Steer serves as a reusable rollout-time action-value wrapper that enhances average molecular optimization reward across different optimizer families and policy backbones without requiring additional online oracle budget

title: Do Latent Channels Actually Communicate? A Causal Audit of Latent Multi-Agent LLM
summary: Latent communication in large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) transmits continuous internal representations instead of text, but greater representational capacity does not establish that the receiver uses task-relevant information. End-task performance alone also cannot reveal whether an observed effect depends on message presence, content generated for the evaluated example, or information supplied by a separate agent. We introduce a causal audit that applies controlled message replacements at the boundary where the sender-produced representation enters the receiver. Four message settings support five measurements of encoded sender information, receiver sensitivity to message presence and identity, the task value of example-specific content, and the additional value supplied by a separate agent. We apply the audit to latent relay with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B on GSM8K, ARC-C, and MATH-500. On GSM8K, the Qwen3-4B overall performance effect of -1.00 percentage point decomposes into a -6.17-point effect retained by an other-example message and a +5.17-point effect attributable to example-specific content; both component directions reverse at 8B. On MATH-500, the Qwen3-4B gain of 15.00 points comprises 8.33 points retained by an other-example message and 6.67 points attributable to example-specific content, while the 8B gain is dominated by the former component. Self-substitution comparisons further show that example-specific content and other-agent value are distinct. These results show that aggregate accuracy does not identify how a latent message affects the receiver and motivate controlled message comparisons as a standard evaluation for latent communication.

AI.tldr: Researchers introduce a causal audit method to analyze how latent (non-text) communication in multi-agent LLM systems actually works, showing that aggregate performance metrics alone don't reveal whether improvements come from message presence, specific content, or separate agents' information.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of latent communication in LLM-based multi-agent systems only measure end-task performance, which can't reveal the actual mechanisms behind observed effects. The problem is that we don't know whether improvements come from: 1) just having a message present, 2) the specific content generated for that example, or 3) information supplied by another agent.
AI.method: The authors propose a causal audit framework using controlled message replacements at the receiver boundary. They use four message settings to measure: 1) encoded sender information, 2) receiver sensitivity to message presence/identity, 3) task value of example-specific content, and 4) additional value from separate agents. They apply this to Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B models on GSM8K, ARC-C, and MATH-500 datasets.
AI.result: On GSM8K, Qwen3-4B showed -1.00pp overall performance, decomposing into -6.17pp from other-example messages and +5.17pp from example-specific content. These directions reversed for 8B. On MATH-500, Qwen3-4B gained 15.00pp total: 8.33pp from other-example messages and 6.67pp from specific content, while 8B gains were dominated by the former. Self-substitution comparisons confirmed distinct effects.
AI.conclusion: Aggregate accuracy doesn't reveal how latent messages affect receivers. The causal audit approach demonstrates that controlled message comparisons should become standard evaluation for latent communication in multi-agent systems, as they expose the actual mechanisms behind performance changes.

title: Flow Map Learning via Nongradient Vector Flow
summary: Diffusion and flow-based models benefit from simple regression losses, but inference incurs significant overhead because sampling requires integration. Consistency models address this by directly learning the flow maps along the ODE trajectory, opening a design space between one-step and many-step approaches. However, existing methods face computational challenges such as requiring model inverses or backpropagation through iterated model calls, and do not always prove that the desired ODE flow map is a solution to the loss. We introduce SGFlow, an approach for learning flow maps that bypasses explicit invertibility constraints and expensive differentiation through model iteration. SGFlow trains a model to compute both the ODE solutions and the implied velocity from scratch by following non-conservative dynamics with a stationary point at the desired flow map. On the CIFAR image benchmark, no single method attains the best FID at every step count: SGFlow attains the best FID at 10 sampling steps and remains competitive with flow matching, Meanflow, and Lagrangian map matching at other step counts, while being the only one with a proven stationary-point guarantee for its stopgrad-based dynamics.

AI.tldr: SGFlow is a new approach for learning flow maps in consistency models that avoids expensive computations like model inverses or backpropagation through iterated model calls, while providing theoretical guarantees on stationary-point convergence.
AI.motivation: Existing consistency models for diffusion/flow-based models face computational challenges including requiring model inverses or backpropagation through iterated model calls, and lack theoretical guarantees that the learned flow maps correspond to the desired ODE solutions.
AI.method: SGFlow trains a model to compute both ODE solutions and implied velocity from scratch by following non-conservative dynamics with a stationary point at the desired flow map, bypassing explicit invertibility constraints and expensive differentiation through model iteration.
AI.result: On CIFAR image benchmark, SGFlow attains the best FID at 10 sampling steps and remains competitive with flow matching, Meanflow, and Lagrangian map matching at other step counts. It's the only method with a proven stationary-point guarantee for its stopgrad-based dynamics.
AI.conclusion: SGFlow provides a computationally efficient alternative for learning flow maps in consistency models with theoretical guarantees, achieving competitive performance on image generation benchmarks while addressing limitations of existing approaches.

title: Property-driven Causal Abstractions for Markov Decision Processes
summary: Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) are widely used as decision-making models, commonly specified over factored state spaces through state variables and their valuations. The exponential blowup in the number of states renders many reasoning tasks in MDPs challenging. Abstractions are promising techniques to reduce MDPs and thus mitigate scalability issues. In this work, we introduce a notion of causality on factored MDPs and a novel property-driven causal abstraction technique that retains many characteristics of the original MDP model. For this, we rely on causal relations over state variable predicates and identify those states that share the same reasons for fulfilling or violating a given abstraction property. We theoretically and empirically compare various causal MDP abstractions using different model types such as MDPs, interval MDPs, or stochastic games. Our evaluation demonstrates the potential of our approach: For several standard benchmarks, we obtain small abstractions that allow us to compute near-optimal policies for the original MDP. Furthermore, our causal abstractions often generalize to related large-scale MDP models.

AI.tldr: Introduces causal abstractions for factored MDPs to reduce state explosion by preserving causal relations, enabling efficient near-optimal policy computation.
AI.motivation: Factored MDPs suffer from exponential state blowup, making reasoning tasks challenging. Existing abstraction techniques need better preservation of original model characteristics for scalability and generalizability.
AI.method: Defines causality on factored MDPs and develops property-driven causal abstraction using causal relations over state variable predicates. Identifies states sharing same reasons for property fulfillment/violation.
AI.result: Produces small abstractions for standard benchmarks enabling near-optimal policy computation. Causal abstractions often generalize to related large-scale MDP models. Theoretical and empirical comparison with MDPs, interval MDPs, and stochastic games.
AI.conclusion: Causal abstraction is a promising technique to combat state explosion in factored MDPs while maintaining model characteristics and enabling generalization across related models.

title: Examining the Efficacy of Graph Neural Network Message-Passing in Regression Contexts
summary:
Graph Neural Networks (GNN) facilitate effective prediction on graph data such as molecules, media networks and neural network blueprints. GNNs facilitate prediction through message passing techniques which define how information flows from a node to its neighbors. Due to the ubiquity of the graph data type, the development of newer and better GNNs has garnered much interest in the machine learning community.
  However, GNN evaluation and benchmarking is primarily driven by classification tasks. Thus, prospective GNN message passing layers are evaluated on their ability to outperform prior work in classification contexts. In contrast, GNNs are equally capable of performing scalar regression prediction, yet this class of problem is often overlooked when proposing new GNNs while the best classification GNNs are utilized in an a priori or off-the-shelf manner for regression problems. In response, this paper studies the efficacy of GNN layers in a slew of regression contexts from rank ordering, error minimization and insight extraction. Results show that deep convolutional GNNs, particularly GEN, are more effective at these tasks than attention-based GNNs, while other classical, theoretically-inspired GNNs remain competitive and efficient.

AI.tldr: GNNs are primarily evaluated on classification tasks, but this paper investigates their effectiveness in scalar regression contexts, finding deep convolutional GNNs outperform attention-based approaches for regression problems.
AI.motivation: Current GNN evaluation is dominated by classification tasks, causing new GNN layers to be optimized for classification performance. However, GNNs are also capable of scalar regression prediction, but regression problems are often overlooked when proposing new GNNs, and classification-optimized GNNs are simply used "off-the-shelf" for regression without proper evaluation.
AI.method: The paper studies GNN layer efficacy in various regression contexts including rank ordering, error minimization, and insight extraction. It compares different types of GNN architectures for regression performance.
AI.result: Deep convolutional GNNs, particularly GEN (Graph Edge Network), are more effective at regression tasks than attention-based GNNs. Other classical, theoretically-inspired GNNs remain competitive and efficient for regression problems.
AI.conclusion: Regression tasks should be given more consideration in GNN development and evaluation, as specialized architectures like deep convolutional GNNs perform better for regression than attention-based models that may excel at classification.

title: From Passive Video to Editable Experience: Physically Grounded Experience Synthesis for Embodied Intelligence
summary: The key bottleneck in embodied AI is not model architecture but data. Although billions of human manipulation videos exist online, robots cannot directly learn from them due to the embodiment gap between human morphology and robot hardware. We introduce Pegasus, a low-resource framework that bridges this gap by translating human demonstrations into robot-learnable data through structured knowledge transfer. Instead of relying on raw video prompts, Pegasus constructs a graph-based intermediate representation: a Task Graph extracted from human videos is transformed through Affordance and Constraint Graphs into a Robot Planning Graph for robot-conditioned video generation. A hierarchical affordance latent space models the relationship between object states, affordances, and tasks, enabling generalization beyond object identities. A closed-loop physics verifier further filters invalid generations using kinematic feasibility, collision constraints, and joint limits. We evaluate Pegasus across a range of egocentric manipulation benchmarks, including GTEA Gaze+ and EPIC-KITCHENS-100, and diverse robot embodiments, assessing Task Correctness, Executability, State Consistency, and Learnability. Results demonstrate reliable cross-embodiment translation and show that robot data generation can be reframed from a hardware collection problem into a scalable, low-resource knowledge transfer problem.

AI.tldr: Pegasus framework bridges human-to-robot embodiment gap through structured knowledge transfer, enabling scalable robot data generation from human videos without hardware-specific data collection.
AI.motivation: The key bottleneck in embodied AI is data, not model architecture. While billions of human manipulation videos exist, robots cannot directly learn from them due to the embodiment gap between human morphology and robot hardware.
AI.method: Pegasus constructs graph-based intermediate representations: Task Graph extracted from human videos → transformed through Affordance and Constraint Graphs → Robot Planning Graph for robot-conditioned video generation. Uses hierarchical affordance latent space for generalization beyond object identities, and closed-loop physics verifier with kinematic feasibility, collision constraints, and joint limits.
AI.result: Evaluated across egocentric manipulation benchmarks (GTEA Gaze+ and EPIC-KITCHENS-100) and diverse robot embodiments, assessing Task Correctness, Executability, State Consistency, and Learnability. Demonstrated reliable cross-embodiment translation.
AI.conclusion: Robot data generation can be reframed from a hardware collection problem into a scalable, low-resource knowledge transfer problem through structured knowledge transfer that bridges the human-robot embodiment gap.

title: SCOUT: Per-Context Reset Curricula for Sparse-Reward Reinforcement Learning
summary: Sparse-reward reinforcement learning often fails because rollouts from the unassisted evaluation start rarely reach later task stages. Reset curricula address this by starting some training rollouts from easier intermediate states, called scaffolds. Such a curriculum faces two decisions: scaffold access, obtaining informative starts, and scaffold allocation, deciding how quickly that assistance is removed. Most prior curricula pace removal on one shared schedule, which can fail when task instances, or contexts, learn at different rates. We introduce SCOUT, an online, learner-agnostic reset controller that gives every context its own curriculum. Using only binary rollout success, SCOUT removes assistance after sustained success, restores it after failure, and cautiously tests a harder start when progress stalls, without changing the reward, optimizer, or learner. A counting construction shows that synchronized global pacing can be insufficient when contexts need conflicting amounts of assisted practice. Across six navigation and manipulation settings, scaffold access improves learning and enables success in three where unassisted training fails within the reported budget. In a constructed pacing conflict, each tested global schedule leaves one group unsolved, while SCOUT solves both. Average success can conceal this failure, so we also report the least successful group. Group-level pacing works when learning differences follow known groups but can fail when they occur within one group. SCOUT needs no group labels and remains consistently strong in both cases. A reset curriculum should remove assistance at the scale where learning progress differs.

AI.tldr: SCOUT is an adaptive reset curriculum controller that provides individualized scaffolding to different task contexts, addressing limitations of global pacing schedules that fail when contexts learn at different rates.
AI.motivation: Sparse-reward RL often fails because initial rollouts rarely reach later task stages. Traditional reset curricula use global pacing schedules that remove assistance uniformly, but these fail when different task contexts learn at different rates, creating pacing conflicts where some contexts get insufficient practice while others get too much assistance.
AI.method: SCOUT is an online, learner-agnostic reset controller that maintains individualized curricula for each context. It uses only binary rollout success to adapt scaffolding: removes assistance after sustained success, restores it after failure, and cautiously tests harder starts when progress stalls. The method doesn't modify rewards, optimizers, or learners.
AI.result: Scaffolding improves learning across six navigation/manipulation settings, enabling success in three where unassisted training fails. In constructed pacing conflicts, global schedules leave one group unsolved while SCOUT solves both. SCOUT performs well both when learning differences follow known groups and when they occur within groups, without needing group labels.
AI.conclusion: Reset curricula should remove assistance at the scale where learning progress differs. SCOUT demonstrates that individualized context-specific curricula outperform global pacing schedules, especially when contexts have conflicting needs for assisted practice, and maintains robust performance without requiring group labels or learner modifications.

title: What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation
comment: 17 pages (11 main + appendices), 7 figures. Accepted at the North East AI Agents Day 2026 workshop, Jane Street, New York City. Workshop: https://ne-agents-day.github.io/
summary: Bot detectors deployed at scale treat traffic as binary: human or bot. This assumption breaks when AI agents browse the web through browser automation, a traffic class that is neither and that binary classifiers structurally cannot represent. We present a three-class detection framework distinguishing humans, bots, and AI agents, and show that the binary-vs-agent confusion is architectural: a binary human-vs-bot detector misroutes agent sessions because its label space lacks an agent class. On our controlled benchmark, an MLP binary classifier misclassifies 39.1% of real AI agents as human and a SAINT binary transformer misclassifies 34.5%; adding an explicit agent class yields per-class agent F1 = 1.000 in all 30 runs (3 model families $\times$ 10 seeds). To measure evasion resistance, we construct a five-level evasion ladder spanning passive observation, GAN-generated trajectories, and replay of real human cursor data ($n = 2299$ evasion sessions). Across 10 seeds and 3 model families we observe zero agent misses in 22990 per-seed predictions.
