AI.method: Proposes amortized moment matching using neural networks to learn data moments as distributional training signals. Casts diffusion denoisers through polynomial projections to establish a general framework for moment amortization. Introduces Amortized Fréchet Distance (AMFD) loss derived from the tractable affine case, using an alternating matrix-free optimization pipeline that dynamically learns conditional moments.
AI.result: AMFD substantially surpasses FD baseline on FDr$^6$ metric and achieves superior one-step generation on ImageNet. When scaled to text-to-image generation, AMFD-enabled one-step models outperform multi-step FLUX.2 4B teachers on GenEval benchmark while achieving on-par performance on PickScore. The method also reveals that first two moments can identify target distributions only in spaces with strong semantics.
AI.conclusion: AMFD provides an efficient, scalable alternative to explicit statistical moment matching for diffusion models, enabling robust training dynamics, superior one-step generation performance, and strong conditional generation capabilities for text-to-image synthesis.

title: Two Calls Beat Five Agents: Evaluating Multi-Agent Pipelines Against Self-Refinement for Local Language Models
summary: Multi-agent LLM pipeline systems break down the task among multiple roles for better reasoning, but are benchmarked mainly with large-scale commercial models. In this study, we investigate Parishad, a structured multi-agent system involving five roles, by deploying it on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, a local model, on two datasets: GSM8K (500 questions) and HumanEval (164 questions), compared with prompting directly and two-call self-refinement. The multi-agent system drops GSM8K accuracy from 75.0\% to 45.0\% with JSON data format due to the error accumulation problem. With plaintext format, the accuracy is restored to 82.0\%. A two-call self-refinement strategy (V1) can achieve 86.2\% accuracy on GSM8K, with 7.4$\times$ lower token usage. However, the same V1 implementation on HumanEval---where direct accuracy is already 96.3\%---actively destroys performance (66.5\%). A task-aware gated redesign (V2) applied to HumanEval preserves accuracy at 95.1\%. Our results demonstrate that communication format and implementation details determine outcomes more than architectural complexity, and that simpler approaches match or outperform multi-agent pipelines for local 7B model deployment. All code and data are released.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent LLM systems using large models often don't work well with local 7B models; simpler 2-call self-refinement with careful formatting can outperform complex multi-agent setups while using significantly fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM pipelines are typically benchmarked with large commercial models, but their effectiveness on smaller local models (like 7B parameter models) is unclear. The researchers want to understand how multi-agent systems perform when deployed on local models with limited capacity.
AI.method: Tested Parishad (a structured multi-agent system with 5 roles) on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct using two datasets: GSM8K (500 math questions) and HumanEval (164 coding questions). Compared three approaches: (1) direct prompting, (2) multi-agent system (JSON and plaintext formats), (3) two-call self-refinement strategies (V1 and task-aware gated V2).
AI.result: Multi-agent system with JSON format dropped GSM8K accuracy from 75.0% to 45.0% due to error accumulation. With plaintext, accuracy recovered to 82.0%. Two-call self-refinement (V1) achieved 86.2% accuracy on GSM8K with 7.4× lower token usage. On HumanEval where direct accuracy was already 96.3%, V1 destroyed performance (66.5%), but task-aware gated V2 preserved accuracy at 95.1%.
AI.conclusion: Communication format and implementation details matter more than architectural complexity for local 7B models. Simpler approaches (like 2-call self-refinement) can match or outperform complex multi-agent pipelines when properly designed, with significantly lower token costs. Task-aware adaptations are crucial for different problem types.

title: Temporally Centered SIGReg Improves Multi-Task LeWorldModel Learning: From Analysis to Method
summary: Recent work on LeWorldModel (LeWM) has shown that the Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularizer (SIGReg) enables stable end-to-end world-model learning from pixels by regularizing the latent marginal distribution toward an isotropic Gaussian, thereby preventing representation collapse. While effective and elegant in single-task settings, this recipe does not extend reliably to multi-task training, leading to substantially worse downstream behavior-cloning performance. In this paper, we show that marginal Gaussianization compresses the separation between task-dependent latent clusters relative to within-cluster variation. This compression introduces representation aliasing across tasks and states, and makes the learned representations highly sensitive to small visual perturbations. To address this problem, we apply SIGReg to temporally centered residuals rather than to the latent marginal distribution. This surrogate target places no direct regularization pressure on the separation among cluster centers, removes the requirement that the full latent follow a single isotropic Gaussian, and retains the anti-collapse effect of SIGReg. On the LIBERO benchmark, our method improves downstream success on the long-horizon suite by 1.7x and raises the average success rate across four suites from 53.2% to 73.6%. Without external pretraining, it slightly outperforms Diffusion Policy trained from scratch and approaches the performance of large-scale pretrained policy baselines. These results reveal a structural incompatibility between marginal Gaussian priors and multi-task latent structure, and provide a simple route toward stable and scalable end-to-end multi-task world-model learning.

AI.tldr: SIGReg works well for single-task world-model learning but fails in multi-task settings due to representation compression; applying SIGReg to temporally centered residuals instead of latent marginals solves this, dramatically improving multi-task performance on LIBERO benchmark.
AI.motivation: The Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularizer (SIGReg) enables stable end-to-end world-model learning in single-task settings but doesn't extend reliably to multi-task training, leading to poor downstream behavior-cloning performance. The authors investigate why this happens and seek to fix it.
AI.method: The paper identifies that marginal Gaussianization compresses separation between task-dependent latent clusters relative to within-cluster variation, causing representation aliasing. To fix this, they apply SIGReg to temporally centered residuals instead of to the latent marginal distribution, which removes pressure on cluster separation while retaining anti-collapse effects.
AI.result: On the LIBERO benchmark, the method improves downstream success on the long-horizon suite by 1.7x and raises average success rate across four suites from 53.2% to 73.6%. Without external pretraining, it slightly outperforms Diffusion Policy trained from scratch and approaches large-scale pretrained policy baselines.
AI.conclusion: There's a structural incompatibility between marginal Gaussian priors and multi-task latent structure. Applying SIGReg to temporally centered residuals provides a simple route toward stable and scalable end-to-end multi-task world-model learning, avoiding representation compression while preventing collapse.

title: Surrogate assisted diversity estimation in neural ensemble search
comment: The paper was presented at the "Artificial Intelligence Applications and Innovations 2026" conference. The final publication is available at https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-032-30612-8_12
summary: Ensembles are a standard way to improve the performance and robustness of deep neural networks, but their effectiveness crucially depends on both the quality and the diversity of individual models. Most neural architecture search (NAS) methods are computationally expensive. Extending them to neural ensemble search (NES), which requires joint optimization of individual architectures and their ensemble composition, leads to an exponential growth of the search space and makes the problem computationally intractable. To address this, we introduce a dual-objective surrogate-guided ensemble search: candidate architectures are represented as directed acyclic graphs, and two surrogate models are trained independently to estimate predictive accuracy and diversity potential. Their combined estimates guide an NES framework that efficiently identifies architectures that are both individually strong and collectively diverse. Our final ensemble achieves competitive or superior performance compared to standard baselines such as Deep Ensembles and Random Search on FashionMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100.

AI.tldr: A neural ensemble search (NES) method that uses dual-objective surrogate models to efficiently find architectures that are both accurate and diverse, achieving competitive performance with standard ensemble methods but with less computational cost.
AI.motivation: Ensembles improve neural network performance but depend on both quality and diversity of individual models. Traditional neural architecture search (NAS) is computationally expensive, and extending it to ensemble search (NES) leads to exponential search space growth and computational intractability.
AI.method: Introduces a dual-objective surrogate-guided ensemble search where candidate architectures are represented as directed acyclic graphs. Two surrogate models are trained independently to estimate predictive accuracy and diversity potential. Their combined estimates guide the NES framework to efficiently identify architectures that are both individually strong and collectively diverse.
AI.result: The final ensemble achieves competitive or superior performance compared to standard baselines such as Deep Ensembles and Random Search on FashionMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 datasets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dual-objective surrogate-guided approach successfully addresses the computational challenge of neural ensemble search by efficiently finding architectures that balance individual performance and collective diversity, leading to effective ensembles with manageable computational requirements.

title: Foundation Models for Face Presentation Attack Detection: A Unified Linear-Probing Benchmark
summary: Face presentation attack detection (PAD) remains challenging under cross-dataset evaluation, where domain shift degrades models trained on a single dataset. The scarcity of large-scale labeled data motivates adapting pretrained vision models rather than training task-specific architectures from scratch, raising a fundamental question: do general-purpose vision foundation models encode PAD-relevant information accessible with minimal task-specific training? To investigate, we systematically evaluate 24 frozen encoders, including self-supervised vision transformers, vision-language encoders, and supervised CNNs, using a unified linear-probing protocol on the MCIO benchmark (MSU-MFSD, CASIA-FASD, Replay-Attack, OULU-NPU). The backbone remains fixed, and only a lightweight linear head is trained to isolate the PAD information already present in the pretrained representation. %We report intra- and cross-dataset performance, along with accuracy-compute trade-offs, relative to two specialist PAD baselines. Results show that frozen foundation-model representations can support strong intra-dataset PAD performance with only a linear classifier, but this performance does not reliably transfer across datasets. Model scale is beneficial within several families, although the effect is not monotonic and is strongly mediated by architecture and pretraining. InternViT-6B achieves the lowest mean intra-dataset error, whereas CLIP ViT-B/32 offers the most favorable cross-dataset transfer-compute trade-off among the evaluated probes. These findings suggest that while pretrained representations contain PAD-relevant information, explicit adaptation remains necessary to address domain shift.

AI.tldr: Frozen vision foundation models contain PAD-relevant information accessible via linear probing, but this information doesn't reliably transfer across datasets, requiring explicit adaptation for domain shift.
AI.motivation: Face presentation attack detection (PAD) faces challenges with cross-dataset evaluation due to domain shift. Since labeled PAD data is scarce, adapting pretrained vision models is attractive. The research investigates whether general-purpose vision foundation models already encode PAD-relevant information that can be accessed with minimal task-specific training.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation of 24 frozen encoders including self-supervised vision transformers, vision-language encoders, and supervised CNNs using unified linear-probing protocol on MCIO benchmark (MSU-MFSD, CASIA-FASD, Replay-Attack, OULU-NPU). Backbones remain fixed, only a lightweight linear head is trained to isolate PAD information already present in pretrained representations.
AI.result: Frozen foundation-model representations support strong intra-dataset PAD performance with just a linear classifier, but this performance doesn't reliably transfer across datasets. Model scale helps within several families, though not monotonically and strongly mediated by architecture and pretraining. InternViT-6B achieves lowest mean intra-dataset error, while CLIP ViT-B/32 offers most favorable cross-dataset transfer-compute trade-off among evaluated probes.
AI.conclusion: While pretrained representations contain PAD-relevant information, explicit adaptation remains necessary to address domain shift for reliable cross-dataset transfer in face presentation attack detection.

title: What Can Latent World Models Know? Physical Parameter Identifiability in Multimodal Predictive Representations
summary: A central premise of latent world models is that predicting the future forces a representation to internalize the physics of its environment. Which physical quantities does a trained latent actually contain, and what decides this? We answer with controlled interventions in POKEWORLD, an interactive environment whose visually identical objects hide mass, drag, and contact stiffness. A certificate-gated protocol first certifies each parameter as recoverable from raw observations, then measures whether it enters the latent, so a null result can be attributed to the objective rather than to the environment. The resulting identifiability map has two organizing mechanisms and one frontier. Inputs limit what can be known, while prediction targets decide what is retained. Stiffness enters the latent only when touch is forecast ($R^2=0.50$, compared with $-0.02$ when the same signal is merely fused into the input), and under single-step prediction a vision-only latent discards even perfectly visible object state. Drag marks the frontier. It carries a recoverability certificate of 0.89 yet plateaus near 0.13 under every deterministic prediction objective we test, while a supervised head on the same trunk reaches 0.45. Parameters whose readout is slow and ratio-type under the sensed coordinates fall outside what these objectives acquire. On RH20T, an input-target factorial across scaling curves reproduces both mechanisms across two robots and 4,258 episodes. Every arm missing information or prediction pressure stays flat over a fivefold data range, and only the full multimodal objective forecasts force beyond a persistence baseline, with held-out gains that grow with scale. Objective structure determines which physical parameters a latent acquires, and additional data improves only the parameters it already acquires.

AI.tldr: Latent world models acquire different physical parameters depending on prediction objectives, not just environmental information availability. Inputs limit what can be known, while prediction targets determine what is retained in the latent representation.
AI.motivation: To understand which physical quantities latent world models actually internalize from their environment, and what factors determine this acquisition process - moving beyond the assumption that simply predicting the future automatically captures all relevant physics.
AI.method: Used controlled interventions in POKEWORLD environment with visually identical objects hiding mass, drag, and stiffness. Developed certificate-gated protocol to first certify parameter recoverability from raw observations, then measure if parameters enter latent. Applied input-target factorial design across scaling curves on RH20T robot dataset to validate findings.
AI.result: Stiffness only enters latent when touch is forecasted (R²=0.50 vs -0.02 when fused into input). Vision-only latents discard visible object state under single-step prediction. Drag shows recoverability certificate of 0.89 but plateaus at 0.13 under deterministic prediction, while supervised head reaches 0.45. Only full multimodal objective forecasts force beyond persistence baseline, with gains growing with scale.
AI.conclusion: Objective structure determines which physical parameters a latent acquires. Inputs limit knowledge, prediction targets determine retention. Additional data only improves parameters already acquired by the objective, not those outside its scope. Some parameters (especially slow, ratio-type ones) fall outside what standard prediction objectives acquire.

title: TreeCCA: Canonical Correlation Analysis via Gradient-Boosted Trees
summary:
Gradient-boosted trees dominate tabular machine learning, yet canonical correlation analysis has always relied on linear or neural encoders. We propose \textbf{TreeCCA}, the first method to train gradient-boosted tree ensembles end-to-end as CCA encoders, inheriting their plug-and-play reliability: no architecture design, familiar hyperparameters, and strong performance with defaults. The technical enabler is the Eckart-Young (EY) loss, which supplies closed-form per-sample gradients that slot directly into any standard GBT library (XGBoost, LightGBM) as a custom objective.
  TreeCCA is the first CCA method to combine nonlinear accuracy with native interpretability: every tree split selects one feature, so gain importances reveal which inputs drive cross-view correlation at no extra cost. We demonstrate these properties on synthetic benchmarks, where TreeCCA matches or exceeds Deep CCA (2.61 vs.\ 2.43 on Signed Power; 2.93 vs.\ 2.89 on Hermite), and on a sparse benchmark with zero linear cross-view covariance, where TreeCCA recovers the true support with $\text{Precision@}S = 1.00$ at $p=50$ while PMD finds no signal. On the UCI HAR sensor-fusion benchmark, TreeCCA achieves comparable accuracy to Deep CCA at $5\times$ lower cost, while XGBoost gain importances directly validate a physics-motivated hypothesis about the data --- an interpretation not readily available with neural encoders. Across five popular tabular multi-view datasets, TreeMCCA consistently matches or exceeds linear CCA in both nonlinear correlation extraction and downstream classification accuracy.

AI.tldr: TreeCCA is the first method to train gradient-boosted trees as CCA encoders end-to-end, combining nonlinear accuracy with native interpretability through feature selection in tree splits.
AI.motivation: Gradient-boosted trees dominate tabular ML but canonical correlation analysis has traditionally relied on linear or neural encoders. There's a gap in having nonlinear CCA with the reliability, ease-of-use, and interpretability of tree ensembles.
AI.method: TreeCCA uses Eckart-Young loss to provide closed-form per-sample gradients that can be used as custom objectives in standard GBT libraries (XGBoost, LightGBM). This enables training tree ensembles end-to-end as CCA encoders without requiring architecture design.
AI.result: TreeCCA matches or exceeds Deep CCA on synthetic benchmarks (2.61 vs. 2.43 on Signed Power; 2.93 vs. 2.89 on Hermite), recovers true support with perfect precision on sparse benchmarks, achieves comparable accuracy to Deep CCA at 5× lower cost on UCI HAR, and consistently matches/exceeds linear CCA across five tabular datasets.
AI.conclusion: TreeCCA successfully bridges the gap between nonlinear correlation analysis and practical ML by bringing gradient-boosted trees to CCA, offering both strong performance and native interpretability through feature importance metrics.

title: Lottery Tickets Are Not Deployment Tickets
summary: Reports on how sparsification, compression, and lottery tickets change model behavior have been mixed in the prior literature, with beneficial effects observed in some studies and adverse effects in others. Moreover, prior work has not considered actual deployment conditions, where decision logic is already fixed for the incumbent. To assess these mixed findings from a practical standpoint, we study the production-replacement question at the deployment level, namely whether an accuracy-matched lottery ticket or another sparse challenger can replace an incumbent dense model without reconfiguring downstream decision logic. We therefore audit a broad, protocol-specific panel of deployment-relevant behaviors spanning calibration, OOD response, class-level reliability, representations, and downstream policy decisions, and summarize clean-accuracy-excluded deviations with a behavioral-compatibility distance. Across extensive experiments, sparse candidates repeatedly recover dense-reference accuracy yet remain behaviorally different; in several study-band-matched settings, LTs also show lower corruption accuracy. In small-gap settings with fixed-threshold policy diagnostics, lottery-ticket replacement changes 7% to 10% of accept--review decisions. This churn creates precisely the burden that drop-in replacement is meant to avoid: reconfiguring and revalidating downstream decision logic. These findings establish the limits of clean-accuracy certification: Establishing compatibility with a fixed incumbent is distinct from attributing churn uniquely to sparsity or treating every measured deviation as harmful. Our theory explains the routing result: Even exact pointwise top-1 agreement cannot bound fixed-threshold decision changes, and small confidence shifts near the operating boundary can generate first-order routing churn.

AI.tldr: Sparse models like lottery tickets may match dense models' clean accuracy but create practical deployment issues by altering model behavior (calibration, OOD response, decisions), causing 7-10% decision churn that requires reconfiguring downstream logic.
AI.motivation: Previous research shows mixed results on how model sparsification affects behavior, and prior work hasn't considered real deployment conditions where decision logic is already fixed. The authors want to assess whether accuracy-matched sparse models can truly replace dense models without changing downstream systems.
AI.method: Study the "production-replacement question" by auditing deployment-relevant behaviors including calibration, OOD response, class-level reliability, representations, and downstream policy decisions. Use a behavioral-compatibility distance to summarize deviations, and conduct extensive experiments comparing sparse candidates (including lottery tickets) to dense incumbents.
AI.result: Sparse models recover dense-reference accuracy but remain behaviorally different. Lottery tickets show lower corruption accuracy in some settings. In fixed-threshold policy diagnostics, lottery-ticket replacement changes 7-10% of accept/review decisions, creating the burden of reconfiguring downstream logic that drop-in replacement aims to avoid.
AI.conclusion: Clean-accuracy certification has limits: compatibility with fixed incumbents is distinct from attributing churn to sparsity alone. Theoretical explanation shows even exact top-1 agreement can't bound decision changes, as small confidence shifts near decision boundaries cause significant routing churn.

title: Single-Beat Cuffless Blood Pressure Estimation Using Ear-PPG and ECG with a Lightweight Hybrid Learning Framework
summary: Continuous cuffless blood pressure (BP) monitoring remains challenging due to motion artifacts, physiological variability, and the limited robustness of conventional pulse transit time (PTT) models under dynamic conditions. Many prior approaches rely on multi-second windows to stabilize estimation, an assumption that is frequently violated during real-world monitoring with intermittent signal corruption. Here, we show that discriminative BP-related information is preserved at the single-beat level and present a lightweight multi-modal wearable framework for continuous BP estimation. The system integrates synchronized chest electrocardiography (ECG) and ear-clip reflectance photoplethysmography, each co-located with a 6-axis inertial measurement unit to provide motion context. We introduce a hybrid learning architecture in which a one-dimensional convolutional neural network extracts a 64-dimensional embedding from individual PPG beats and fuses it with 30 physiology-grounded features, including PTT statistics and heart rate variability, followed by LightGBM regression. The method was evaluated using a multi-phase stress protocol ($n=10$) and the PulseDB public dataset with subject-disjoint validation. Across 30 independent runs, the model achieved mean absolute errors of $4.02 \pm 0.21$~mmHg for systolic BP and $1.79 \pm 0.05$~mmHg for diastolic BP, corresponding to a 28.2\% reduction in combined MAE relative to baseline models. By enabling beat-wise estimation without long temporal context, this framework supports computationally efficient cuffless BP monitoring suitable for wearable deployment under practical resource constraints. The source code for this work is available at https://github.com/SYMBIOX-Lab/BP-wireless.

AI.tldr: A lightweight wearable system combining ECG and ear-clip PPG with motion sensors enables single-beat blood pressure estimation using hybrid CNN-feature extraction and LightGBM regression, achieving significant accuracy improvements over baseline methods.
AI.motivation: Continuous cuffless blood pressure monitoring faces challenges from motion artifacts, physiological variability, and limited robustness of conventional PTT models. Existing approaches require multi-second windows that are often violated in real-world settings with intermittent signal corruption.
AI.method: The system integrates synchronized chest ECG and ear-clip reflectance PPG, each co-located with 6-axis IMUs for motion context. A hybrid learning architecture uses a 1D CNN to extract 64-dimensional embeddings from individual PPG beats, which are fused with 30 physiology-grounded features (including PTT statistics and heart rate variability), followed by LightGBM regression.
AI.result: Evaluated on a multi-phase stress protocol (n=10) and PulseDB dataset with subject-disjoint validation, the model achieved MAEs of 4.02 ± 0.21 mmHg for systolic BP and 1.79 ± 0.05 mmHg for diastolic BP over 30 independent runs, representing a 28.2% reduction in combined MAE relative to baseline models.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables beat-wise estimation without requiring long temporal context, supporting computationally efficient cuffless BP monitoring suitable for wearable deployment under practical resource constraints. This addresses key limitations of conventional approaches while maintaining accuracy.

title: Equilibrium Training of Energy-Based Models with Parallel Trajectory Tempering
summary: Energy-Based Models (EBMs) provide an interpretable framework for generative modeling of scientific data, but poor Markov Chain Monte Carlo mixing often limits their reliability. We introduce a training algorithm based on Parallel Trajectory Tempering (PTT), which exploits the continuity of the optimization path to maintain equilibrium sampling throughout learning. This enables stable and fast training on highly multimodal and data-scarce scientific datasets. Combined with reservoir sampling and adaptive optimization, PTT has a computational cost comparable to Persistent Contrastive Divergence, making it a practical replacement for standard training methods. It also provides direct estimates of thermalization times, equilibrium samples from trained models, and accurate log-likelihoods at essentially no additional cost. Experiments on Restricted Boltzmann Machines show that PTT consistently outperforms existing EBM training approaches. On discrete tabular data, it also surpasses state-of-the-art deep generative models, yielding higher-quality samples and greater robustness to overfitting and limited data. Our results make equilibrium maximum-likelihood training of EBMs practical and computationally efficient.

AI.tldr: Introduces Parallel Trajectory Tempering (PTT), a practical and efficient training algorithm for Energy-Based Models that maintains equilibrium sampling throughout learning, outperforming existing methods on both RBMs and discrete tabular data.
AI.motivation: Energy-Based Models are interpretable for scientific data generation but suffer from poor Markov Chain Monte Carlo mixing during training, which limits their reliability and practical use.
AI.method: Proposes Parallel Trajectory Tempering (PTT) training algorithm that exploits continuity of optimization paths to maintain equilibrium sampling, combined with reservoir sampling and adaptive optimization for computational efficiency comparable to Persistent Contrastive Divergence.
AI.result: PTT consistently outperforms existing EBM training approaches on Restricted Boltzmann Machines, surpasses state-of-the-art deep generative models on discrete tabular data, yields higher-quality samples, and shows greater robustness to overfitting and limited data.
AI.conclusion: PTT makes equilibrium maximum-likelihood training of EBMs practical and computationally efficient while providing direct estimates of thermalization times, equilibrium samples, and accurate log-likelihoods at minimal additional cost.

title: Sky sphere representation in language models
summary:
We analyze whether language models of size ~100B have a representation of the night sky map that is decodable from their residual stream. We find that most of the considered open-source models do have such a representation, and it often even surfaces to the top principal components on prompts that ask questions like ``what is close to this object in the night sky''. In all but one model this representation showed significant scores in LOO testing, containing up to 65-85% of variance ($R^2$-score) and having median angular error down to $12^\circ-21^\circ$. We verify that our representation is not a simple leak from a correlated flat representation. To our knowledge, this representation is the first example of a curved high-dimensional irreducible feature manifold.
  Codes used in the paper are published at https://github.com/l3erdnik/Decodable-sky

AI.tldr: Language models (~100B parameters) have a surprisingly accurate, decodable representation of the night sky map in their residual streams, representing the first known example of a curved high-dimensional irreducible feature manifold.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether large language models internally develop meaningful representations of physical spatial relationships, specifically whether they can encode accurate positional information about celestial objects in the night sky.
AI.method: Analyzed residual streams of open-source language models (~100B parameters) using prompts asking about spatial relationships of celestial objects. Applied principal component analysis, leave-one-out testing, and R²-score calculations to measure representation quality. Verified the representation wasn't just a simple leak from correlated flat representations.
AI.result: Most models contained a decodable night sky representation, often appearing in top principal components. Representations showed significant LOO test scores with 65-85% variance explained (R²) and median angular errors of 12°-21°. The representation constitutes a curved high-dimensional irreducible feature manifold rather than a simple flat projection.
AI.conclusion: Large language models can develop surprisingly accurate internal representations of complex physical spatial relationships like celestial positions, demonstrating they learn structured feature manifolds that go beyond simple statistical correlations.

title: Hierarchical Spatio-Temporal Transformer for Coherent Emergency Department Forecasting
comment: Accepted at 11th Workshop on Data Science for Social Good - ECML PKDD 2026
summary: Emergency Departments (EDs) are critical access points in healthcare systems, yet they face persistent pressure from unpredictable patient demand, seasonal surges, and non-urgent visits. Effective ED planning requires forecasts at multiple decision-making levels: hospitals need local demand estimates for staffing and bed management, regions require forecasts to coordinate healthcare units, and national authorities need system-wide projections for capacity planning. However, most existing approaches forecast ED demand independently at a single level, ignoring the hierarchy linking hospitals, regions, and national systems. This can produce incoherent predictions, where hospital-level forecasts do not aggregate consistently to regional or national demand. We propose HierSTT, a hierarchical Transformer-based framework for coherent multi-level ED forecasting. HierSTT jointly predicts hospital, regional, and national level demand in a single end-to-end model. A Temporal Fusion Transformer captures national dynamics, while spatio-temporal Transformer encoder-decoder modules model regional and hospital demand conditioned on higher-level forecasts. A coherence-aware loss penalizes cross-level inconsistencies during training. We further introduce a nationwide Portuguese ED dataset covering 81 hospitals across 5 regional health administrations, with heterogeneous covariates at each level. Experiments show that HierSTT reduces average WAPE by 32\% relative to the best non-hierarchical deep learning baseline and outperforms all classical hierarchical reconciliation methods, while producing near-coherent predictions across levels. Additional resources associated with this work are available at https://github.com/FilipaLino/HierSTT.

AI.tldr: HierSTT: A hierarchical Transformer framework for coherent multi-level emergency department demand forecasting that jointly predicts hospital, regional, and national levels in a single end-to-end model.
AI.motivation: Emergency Departments face pressure from unpredictable demand, seasonal surges, and non-urgent visits. Existing approaches forecast ED demand independently at single levels (hospital, region, or national), ignoring hierarchical relationships. This leads to incoherent predictions where lower-level forecasts don't aggregate consistently to higher levels.
AI.method: HierSTT uses a hierarchical Transformer-based framework with: 1) Temporal Fusion Transformer for national dynamics, 2) spatio-temporal Transformer encoder-decoder modules for regional and hospital demand conditioned on higher-level forecasts, and 3) coherence-aware loss that penalizes cross-level inconsistencies during training.
AI.result: On a nationwide Portuguese ED dataset covering 81 hospitals across 5 regional health administrations, HierSTT reduces average Weighted Absolute Percentage Error (WAPE) by 32% relative to best non-hierarchical deep learning baseline, outperforms all classical hierarchical reconciliation methods, and produces near-coherent predictions across levels.
AI.conclusion: HierSTT provides an effective framework for coherent multi-level ED demand forecasting that addresses the hierarchical nature of healthcare systems while improving accuracy over existing approaches, enabling better resource allocation and capacity planning across hospital, regional, and national levels.

title: Voronoi Histograms for Adaptive Vectorization of Expected Persistence Diagrams
summary: Persistence Diagram (PD) is known to capture point cloud topology effectively, but its computation has high time complexity. Expected Persistence Diagram (EPD) has been developed to reduce the time cost by studying the topology of multiple subsets of a point cloud and it serves as a distribution of topological features. Existing EPD vectorizations often rely on predefined point transformations, such as Gaussian or landscape functions. We study an alternative discretization based on Voronoi histograms, which trades smooth functional approximation for adaptive partition-based counting. We propose to use Voronoi Diagram-based histogram as the vectorization of EPD, without imposing an explicit smooth point transformation model. Under stated separation and normalization conditions, we establish stability bounds and characterize when the histogram representation preserves Wasserstein-scale variation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed representation on real-world datasets which have significant topological features for classification and dimensionality reduction tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using Voronoi diagram-based histograms as an alternative vectorization method for Expected Persistence Diagrams, trading smooth functional approximations for adaptive partition-based counting to capture topological features more effectively.
AI.motivation: Persistence Diagrams effectively capture point cloud topology but have high computational costs. Expected Persistence Diagrams were developed to reduce time complexity by studying multiple subsets, but existing vectorizations rely on predefined smooth transformations (like Gaussian or landscape functions) which may not be optimal for all cases.
AI.method: The authors propose using Voronoi diagram-based histograms as the vectorization method for EPDs, without imposing explicit smooth point transformation models. This approach trades smooth functional approximation for adaptive partition-based counting.
AI.result: The method establishes stability bounds under separation and normalization conditions, characterizes when histogram representations preserve Wasserstein-scale variation, and demonstrates effectiveness on real-world datasets for classification and dimensionality reduction tasks involving significant topological features.
AI.conclusion: Voronoi histogram-based vectorization provides a viable alternative to smooth functional approximations for Expected Persistence Diagrams, offering theoretical guarantees and practical effectiveness for topological data analysis tasks.

title: Minimal Markovization via Stable Quotients in Holonomy-Cover Decision Processes
summary: An agent acting under partial observability must retain a recursively updateable statistic of history that restores the Markov property, but the smallest such statistic is generally unknown. We characterize this minimal Markov sufficient statistic for holonomy-cover decision processes, a structured POMDP class in which the visible dynamics are Markov and every realized visible transition applies a fixed permutation to a hidden mode. In particular, we construct the stable quotient, the coarsest observation-wise abstraction preserving one-step rewards and quotient successors, and prove that the pair of the current observation and stable class forms an exact finite Markov state. When the current class is correctly initialized, exact class tracking requires exactly the minimal memory symbols, in the sense that under reachability and pairwise decision separation at a maximizing observation, no arbitrary finite-memory controller can use fewer. Under resettable diagnostics, nearest-prototype class inference has exponentially decaying error, and a calibrate-then-restart reduction transfers finite-MDP guarantees to the recovered state. The results enable \emph{Holonomy Memory Reinforcement Learning}. It represents memory by the current stable class, updates it through ordered edge transports, identifies local class coordinates when diagnostics are available, and applies a standard finite-MDP RL backbone after synchronization. Experiments recover an exact compression from raw states to quotient states and achieve perfect paired-order accuracy with three decision-time memory states, matching the quotient oracle and outperforming the non-oracle baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper characterizes the minimal Markov sufficient statistic for holonomy-cover decision processes and enables Holonomy Memory Reinforcement Learning that uses stable class tracking for exact state compression.
AI.motivation: In partially observable environments, agents need memory to maintain Markov statistics, but the minimal sufficient statistic is generally unknown. The paper aims to find and characterize this minimal Markov state for structured POMDPs called holonomy-cover decision processes.
AI.method: The authors construct the "stable quotient" - the coarsest observation-wise abstraction preserving one-step rewards and quotient successors. They prove that the pair of current observation and stable class forms an exact finite Markov state. They develop Holonomy Memory Reinforcement Learning that represents memory by current stable class, updates through ordered edge transports, and applies standard finite-MDP RL after synchronization.
AI.result: Experiments show exact compression from raw states to quotient states with perfect paired-order accuracy using only three decision-time memory states, matching the quotient oracle and outperforming non-oracle baselines. The approach achieves exponentially decaying error in class inference under resettable diagnostics.
AI.conclusion: The stable quotient provides the minimal Markov sufficient statistic for holonomy-cover decision processes, enabling exact finite-state representations. Holonomy Memory RL effectively recovers this representation and transfers finite-MDP guarantees to partially observable settings through calibration and restart mechanisms.

title: Skillful forecasting of offshore winds from satellite scatterometer constellations
summary: Accurate intraday forecasts of offshore wind are becoming increasingly important for power system operation and the integration of growing shares of offshore wind energy. Operational forecasts rely predominantly on numerical weather prediction (NWP), which is not optimized for lead times of minutes to hours, where initial-condition accuracy dominates forecast skill. Although satellite scatterometer observations are routinely assimilated into NWP, they have not previously been used directly for forecasting. Here we present WindCastNet, the first satellite-based nowcasting framework for offshore wind speed and direction, introducing a new paradigm for intraday forecasting that learns from spatiotemporally irregular satellite observations. WindCastNet predicts offshore wind fields from observations acquired by satellite scatterometer constellations. WindCastNet employs a partial convolutional long short-term memory network that exploits microwave radar observations from the European, Chinese, and Indian scatterometers despite their irregular spatial coverage, asynchronous sampling, and variable revisit times. Spatial observation masks and inter-observation intervals are encoded, while a continuous temporal representation enables forecasts at arbitrary lead times. Evaluated over the North Sea, WindCastNet reduces the root-mean-square error by 23% and 7% relative to the HARMONIE MEPS model at lead times of 1 and 2 h, respectively, and outperforms persistence by 9-15% during the first three forecast hours. Forecast skill decreases under strong-wind conditions and spatially non-uniform flow. These results demonstrate that satellite scatterometer constellations can provide an independent and competitive source of short-term offshore wind forecasts, opening new opportunities for renewable energy forecasting but also broader marine weather applications, including tropical cyclone nowcasting.

AI.tldr: WindCastNet is a satellite-based nowcasting framework that uses irregular satellite scatterometer observations to forecast offshore wind speed and direction, outperforming traditional NWP models for short lead times.
AI.motivation: Accurate intraday offshore wind forecasts are crucial for power system operation and integrating growing shares of offshore wind energy. Current operational forecasts rely on numerical weather prediction (NWP), which isn't optimized for lead times of minutes to hours where initial-condition accuracy is most important. Satellite scatterometer observations, while assimilated into NWP, have never been used directly for forecasting.
AI.method: WindCastNet employs a partial convolutional long short-term memory (LSTM) network that learns from spatiotemporally irregular satellite observations from European, Chinese, and Indian scatterometer constellations. The system handles irregular spatial coverage, asynchronous sampling, and variable revisit times by encoding spatial observation masks and inter-observation intervals. It uses a continuous temporal representation that enables forecasts at arbitrary lead times.
AI.result: Evaluated over the North Sea, WindCastNet reduces root-mean-square error by 23% and 7% relative to the HARMONIE MEPS model at lead times of 1 and 2 hours respectively, and outperforms persistence by 9-15% during the first three forecast hours. Forecast skill decreases under strong-wind conditions and spatially non-uniform flow.
AI.conclusion: Satellite scatterometer constellations can provide an independent and competitive source of short-term offshore wind forecasts, introducing a new paradigm for intraday forecasting. This opens new opportunities for renewable energy forecasting and broader marine weather applications, including tropical cyclone nowcasting.

title: When Do Learned Diffusion Proposals Help Constraint Solving? A Controlled Study on Continuous Algebraic Systems
summary: Solving a continuous algebraic constraint system requires two decisions: which values satisfy the constraints, and which structural augmentation renders an unsolvable system solvable. Classical solvers answer the first well and the second only by enumeration. On that discrete decision, a candidate-conditioned repair ranker choosing among K augmentations reaches the exhaustive-search ceiling at a fraction of the calls, outperforming random (0.997 vs 0.236 balanced nonlinear menu accuracy; p < 10^-70; 0.982 +/- 0.006 across seeds) and beating a budget-matched per-candidate probe on accuracy and cost. MARC turns such a system into a factor graph, over which a graph-neural diffusion denoiser proposes assignments, descent on an exact computer-algebra energy polishes them, and an exact symbolic checker certifies solutions. Evaluations of diffusion-based proposals rarely include one control: random multi-start under the same refinement budget. Applied to our system, it sharply curtails what the learned proposal contributes on the value decision. Does it beat random multi-start at choosing satisfying assignments? Only narrowly, in a predictable regime. Across trapped low-dimensional families it ties with random restart, but dominates in high dimension, where random search fails. Once variables couple, the advantage is gone. Since all methods share one polish and one checker, best-of-K random multi-start succeeds with probability exactly 1 - (1 - q(n))^K, where q(n) is single-start reachability; one measured constant, with no free parameters, reproduces the entire curve (mean absolute error 0.012). The favorable regime is not specific to our synthetic families: across eight real-world systems in robotics, positioning, optimization, and algebra, classical multi-start solved all eight, none in the learning-favorable regime. We map the regimes in which learned proposals improve solvers.

AI.tldr: A paper analyzing when learned proposals outperform random multi-start methods for solving continuous algebraic constraint systems, showing learned methods only narrowly beat random search in high-dimensional cases but fail to beat it when variables couple, with classical solvers performing well on real-world systems.
AI.motivation: Classical algebraic constraint solvers handle constraint satisfaction well but struggle with structural augmentation decisions, typically using enumeration. The paper aims to determine when learned proposals (like diffusion denoisers) actually outperform simpler random multi-start approaches for solving such systems.
AI.method: The paper introduces MARC, which transforms constraint systems into factor graphs, uses a graph-neural diffusion denoiser to propose assignments, refines them via gradient descent on computer-algebra energy, and certifies solutions with exact symbolic checking. The key methodological innovation is comparing against a proper control: random multi-start with the same refinement budget.
AI.result: Learned proposals only narrowly beat random multi-start in predictable high-dimensional regimes, tie with random restart in low-dimensional families, and lose their advantage when variables couple. Across eight real-world systems (robotics, positioning, optimization, algebra), classical multi-start solved all eight, with none in the learning-favorable regime. The exact probability formula 1 - (1 - q(n))^K accurately predicts random multi-start success.
AI.conclusion: The favorable regime for learned proposals is limited to high-dimensional cases where random search fails, but they don't outperform random multi-start when variables couple. Real-world problems often fall outside the learning-favorable regime, making classical multi-start competitive or superior. The work maps when learned methods actually improve solvers versus when they offer minimal advantage.

title: Inverse Learning of Latent Risk-Neutral Densities from Irregular Option Quotes
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF 2026)
summary: Accurate option prices do not imply accurate recovery of the latent risk-neutral density. We study this distinction with two complementary benchmarks. A controlled benchmark exposes simulator-truth densities for latent evaluation, while a chronological NIFTY benchmark tests only held-out market prices. A two-component lognormal mixture has the lowest aggregate price, $L^1$, Wasserstein, and fixed-tail errors on the synthetic benchmark. Learned operators retain narrower strengths: DeepONet reduces 1% quantile and variance error by 39.0% and 34.6% relative to the mixture, and a quote transformer reduces $L^1$ by 16.4% on the structurally misspecified Merton family. A numerical conditioning analysis explains why these rankings can differ: after enforcing mass and forward constraints, 95 of 126 pricing directions are numerically null, and two densities separated by $L^1 = 0.061$ produce identical prices on the covered strikes. On 524 held-out NIFTY calls, validation-selected test-time adaptation reduces DeepONet RMSE by 28.3%, but per-expiry mixture and SVI fits remain much more accurate. The evidence supports target-dependent inductive bias, not a universal winner.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that accurate option pricing doesn't guarantee accurate recovery of risk-neutral densities, revealing a "price-density gap" where different densities can produce identical option prices due to numerical conditioning issues.
AI.motivation: There's a fundamental distinction between accurately pricing options and accurately recovering the underlying risk-neutral density, which is crucial for risk management and derivative pricing but often overlooked when evaluating models solely on pricing performance.
AI.method: Uses two complementary benchmarks: (1) a controlled synthetic benchmark with known ground-truth densities for latent evaluation, and (2) a chronological NIFTY benchmark testing only held-out market prices. Compares mixture models, DeepONet, and transformer approaches, with numerical conditioning analysis and test-time adaptation.
AI.result: The two-component lognormal mixture performs best overall on synthetic benchmarks, while specialized models show narrower strengths. Numerical conditioning reveals that 95 of 126 pricing directions are null after constraints, and densities differing by L¹=0.061 can produce identical option prices. On NIFTY data, validation-selected test-time adaptation reduces DeepONet RMSE by 28.3%, but mixture and SVI fits remain more accurate.
AI.conclusion: There is no universal best model; the evidence supports target-dependent inductive bias, where different models excel at different tasks (pricing vs. density recovery), and the "price-density gap" highlights limitations of evaluating models solely on pricing performance.

title: From Classification to Regression: Using a Fruitfly to Solve Equations
summary: We present a novel approach to regression tasks using classification which is motivated by the mechanism used by fruitflies to sense their environment. Specifically, we formulate a general framework for learning nonlinear input-output relationships by replacing complex global surrogate models with a finite library of representative local patterns. Since scientific data often occupy limited and recurring regions of the input space, we generate predictions by measuring similarities between a query and stored patterns, then combining their associated responses through weighted reconstruction. We apply this approach to nonlinear dynamical systems, data-driven regression, and physics-informed learning using suitable embeddings and similarity measures. For dynamical systems, our offline-online workflow extracts patterns from data or governing equations during the offline phase, while online prediction requires only similarity evaluation and response aggregation. This structure helps us reduce computational and memory demands while providing explicit control over the trade-off among accuracy, storage, and inference cost.

AI.tldr: A classification-based regression framework inspired by fruitfly sensing, using local pattern libraries instead of global models for efficient nonlinear function approximation.
AI.motivation: Motivated by how fruitflies sense their environment, and addressing the challenge that scientific data often occupies limited, recurring regions of input space. Need for efficient learning of nonlinear relationships without complex global models.
AI.method: Replace complex global surrogate models with finite library of representative local patterns. For query prediction: measure similarities between query and stored patterns, then combine associated responses through weighted reconstruction. Applied to nonlinear dynamical systems, data-driven regression, and physics-informed learning with appropriate embeddings and similarity measures.
AI.result: Offline-online workflow for dynamical systems: offline phase extracts patterns from data/governing equations; online prediction only needs similarity evaluation and response aggregation. Provides explicit control over accuracy-storage-inference cost trade-off while reducing computational and memory demands.
AI.conclusion: The biologically-inspired pattern library approach offers an efficient alternative to traditional regression methods, particularly suitable for scientific data that occupies limited input regions, with controllable trade-offs between accuracy, storage, and computational cost.

title: Do You Really Need to Pretrain Q-Functions for Online RL Fine-Tuning?
summary: Pre-training followed by fine-tuning has become the dominant recipe for learning performant policies, and in value-based reinforcement learning (RL) this raises a natural question: given a pretrained policy, should the Q-function be pretrained on offline data too? Conventional wisdom suggests it should, but recent results show that online RL with a randomly-initialized Q-function can result in highly performant and reliable policies without needing to pretrain the Q-function. In this paper, we systematically study whether pretraining the Q-function actually helps when fine-tuning on top of a pretrained base policy. We find, surprisingly, that naive Q-function pretraining often provides little benefit over random initialization. We show this stems from a fundamental mismatch: the Q-function learned during pretraining targets the pretrained policy's Q-function, not the Q-function that online fine-tuning converges to, and this gap persists even after offline value maximization. Motivated by this finding, we propose Initialization via Policy Ensemble (IPE), a simple method that trains multiple diverse policies and uses their pooled rollouts to bootstrap the Q-function learning in online RL. Across a suite of challenging continuous control benchmarks, IPE yields an average 1.26x improvement in fine-tuning performance over naive Q-function pre-training.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that pretraining Q-functions doesn't help much for fine-tuning pretrained policies, proposes a method (IPE) using policy ensembles to bootstrap Q-learning, and achieves 1.26x better performance.
AI.motivation: In value-based RL with pre-training then fine-tuning, there's uncertainty about whether Q-functions should also be pretrained on offline data. Conventional wisdom says yes, but recent results show random initialization can work well. The paper aims to systematically study if Q-function pretraining actually helps with fine-tuning pretrained policies.
AI.method: The authors propose Initialization via Policy Ensemble (IPE), which trains multiple diverse policies and uses their pooled rollouts to bootstrap Q-function learning in online RL, rather than naive pretraining of Q-functions on offline data.
AI.result: Surprisingly, naive Q-function pretraining often provides little benefit over random initialization. The proposed IPE method yields an average 1.26x improvement in fine-tuning performance over naive Q-function pre-training across challenging continuous control benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Q-function pretraining isn't as helpful as expected due to a fundamental mismatch between pretrained Q-functions and what online fine-tuning converges to. IPE provides a better initialization method by leveraging diverse policy ensembles to bootstrap Q-learning, offering significant performance improvements for fine-tuning pretrained policies.
